Title: Combined discussion on the Budget (General) for 2005-2006 and Demands for Grants on Account for 2005-2006 and Supplementary Demands for Grants for 2005-2006. ( Concluded). 

13.09 hrs.

GENERAL BUDGET, 2005-2006 - GENERAL DISCUSSION

DEMANDS FOR GRANTS ON ACCOUNT – (GENERAL) 2005-2006 

AND

DEMANDS FOR SUPPLEMENTARY GRANTS – (GENERAL) 2004-2005 

MR. SPEAKER: Hon. Members, as you know, the discussion on the General Budget is still continuing. The reply will be given by the hon. Minister at 5 p.m. I would request the hon. Members to participate in the discussion within that time. Hon. Members who are not able to participate because of lack of time, may submit their written speeches, which will be taken on record. 

Now, Shri P.S. Gadhavi to continue his speech.

13.10 hrs. (Mr. Deputy-Speaker in the Chair)

SHRI P.S. GADHAVI (KUTCH): I thank the hon. Speaker for giving me this opportunity. Yesterday I rose to oppose the Budget for the year 2005-06. I was telling yesterday as to how Shri C.P. Chandrasekhar described this Budget. In the "Front Line" dated 25th March, 2005, Shri C.P. Chandrasekhar described this Budget as "down-size and go-off Budget". He has further stated that the hon. Finance Minister has been caught between the desire to see India as a globalising economy with a fiscally prudent Government and the compulsion to pay obeisance to goals rendered imperative by democracy, coalition politics and the National Common Minimum Programme. By this Budget, the hon. Finance Minister has emerged more as a manipulator of accounts than as a prudent Finance Minister. 

Sir, can this Budget be said to be a Budget for an Aam Admi  as it is claimed by the hon. Finance Minister?   In hopes, it is ‘yes’ but in realism, it is ‘no’. As this Budget is full of half truths and half-baked reforms, what hurts the 

Aam Admi  in this Budget is that there is lack of transparency in respect of several statements of the hon.Finance Minister. 

The first one is about bringing out customs duty to the level of ASEAN rates though the expression used is "East Asian Neighbours." Further, the Budget says: "Therefore, non-agricultural peak rate is being reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent." This is not really what the Asian rate structure is. The Asian rate is an under-weighted average of industrial and agricultural rates put together. An under-weighted average of customs duties in India is still at the level of 25 per cent or so because, we have got rates like 150 per cent, 100 per cent, 90 per cent, 85 per cent, 80 per cent and so on. Unless all these rates are brought down and the average comes to 15 per cent, one cannot say that we have come near the Asian structure.

The second instance of lack of transparency is the claim that the excise duty for iron and steel has been raised from 10 per cent to 16 per cent but this should have little effect on the prices because the entire duty is MODVATable by most categories of consumers. This is not correct. I say this because it is not MODVATable when sold to building and road building industry. The percentage of such sale is very high, nearly 40 per cent. What is most important is that even where the duty is MODVATed, ultimately, the incidence of the higher duty is passed on finally to the consumer. He has to pay more and, therefore, the prices will rise.

The third example I may give is that a suggestion had been made that the scope of power of Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) should not be limited only to the non-residents and joint ventures with NRIs but should be extended to cover the ordinary Indian manufacturers and importers. What has been done on the other hand is to extend the power only to the existing joint ventures in India. This is hardly an effective extension of the power. What the Budget has forgotten is an average Indian manufacturer or importer. He also needs certainty and he is being denied of this. This is extremely disappointing. So, this Budget has not even adhered to the CMP. I say this because in the CMP, it was promised to give the National Employment Guarantee Scheme. This Scheme has been whittled down to just a Rural Employment Scheme, excluding the urban poor. What about the urban poor? Why are they being denied of this? This has also excluded the majority of districts in the country. For these districts, where is the promise of the CMP? Even for this whittled down, diluted Scheme, the Budget provides a sum of only Rs.11,000 crore. 

Moreover, instead of promoting and protecting the Small Scale Industries (SSIs), as laid down in the CMP, the hon. Finance Minister has de-reserved as many as 108 industries from the SSI List. This has made the position of SSIs, of which thousands are sick, even more unviable.

In the NCMP, the outlay on education was to be increased to six per cent of the GDP. Even after the education cess was levied in last year’s Budget, it has gone up to only Rs.19,119 crore out of a Budget of Rs.5,14,344 crore. Out of this, the outlay for secondary and higher education will be only Rs.2,712 crore.

The hon. Finance Minister has dutifully cited Dr. Amartya Sen and the need to emulate, Cambridge, Oxford and Yale, but ended up giving only one institution of higher education, that is, the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, with a one time grant of Rs.100 crore.

Similarly in the health sector, according to the NCMP, the outlay was to go up to two per cent of the GDP, but the outlay for health and family welfare is only Rs.9,682 crore out of the total outlay of Rs.5,14,344 crore.

Similarly, the hon. Finance Minister promised to make Mumbai a regional hub for finance. For this too, no money has been given and only a proposal has been given for a high powered expert committee to advise the Government.

Further, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill is promised in this Session. 

It is also incorrect to dub this Budget as a ‘Middle Class Budget’. This is, in fact, a pro rich Budget. It is a favourable reaction of business lobbies and the share market. Take the case of direct taxes. The domestic corporate pays 30 per cent income tax, plus a surcharge of ten per cent, so does an individual with an annual income of over Rs.2.5 lakh pays the same rate minus the surcharge. So, the upper middle class is paying the same rate as the corporate sector.

I appreciate hon. Finance Minister for making provision for water shortage in Chennai, in his last Budget and giving special status to Kochi Port. But I would have congratulated him, if he would have considered in this Budget, the demand and requirements of other parts of the country, which are facing acute shortage of drinking water. My constituency, that is, Kutch in Gujarat, is facing acute shortage of water for drinking, agriculture and for industrial purposes. The hon. Finance Minister should have given more impetus for further development of Kandla Port, which is on the western shore, as he has given to Kochi Port. The Government needs to pay more attention to Kandla Port.

I would request the hon. Finance Minister to consider the request of Gujarat Government so that the outstanding Central loan to Gujarat Government be restructured to a rate of interest of not more than seven per cent.

Secondly, the Sardar Sarovar Project of Gujarat is a multi-State project with benefits of irrigation and power to Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. It is a fact that this project has suffered heavy cost over-runs due to delay caused by anti-dam activism. The original cost of the dam was Rs.6,406.04 crore at 1986-87 price level. It went up to Rs.27,462.66 crore at 2000-01 price level. Therefore, the Central Government should reimburse the State Government, by way of a special grant, the cost of interest on the project.

I would also urge upon the hon. Finance Minister to consider the request of Gujarat Government to grant exemption to Gujarat Maritime Board from the payment of income tax considering it as a local authority. Now, it is not considered as local authority, therefore, the Gujarat Maritime Board, which is a Government body, is required to pay income tax. So, I would request the hon. Finance Minister to consider this request of the Gujarat Government.

I further request the hon. Finance Minister to consider the request of Gujarat Government to scrap the five per cent customs duty on recycling scrap of old vessels at Alang Ship Breaking Yard because Government of India has scraped the five per cent customs duty on imported melting scrap. They are liable to pay five per cent duty, but if it is imported, they are not required to pay any duty.

So, in Alang Ship Breaking Yard, if whatever ship comes and it is recycled, those scraps may not have any duty. 

I also request the hon. Finance Minister to consider this. In the past, two per cent surcharge was levied on income tax for the earthquake-stricken people of Gujarat. That amount remains with the Central Government. The unpaid amount should be paid back to the Gujarat Government. 

Lastly, I conclude by saying that rhetorical flourishes and generous promises are no substitute for resolute political will and a commitment to the economic well being of the people. Both are conspicuously missing in this Budget.

*SHRI N.S.V. CHITTHAN (DINDIGUL): I would like to compliment and congratulate our Finance Minister, Shri P. Chidambaram for having dedicated to this nation a far-sighted, growth-oriented, rural-based dream Budget. This is the second Budget of the U.P.A. Government guided by Madam Soniaji and led by Dr. Manmohan Singh. 

It is literally a dream Budget because it is poised to make the common man’s dream come true. The farmer will have more money in his kitty. Industry is happy and business is brimming with confidence. More importantingly, the housewife is glad. So, in a way, the Union Budget has satisfied everyone except, of course, the Opposition. The Opposition is disappointed not because the Budget was not good but because they could not find any fault. So, we can understand their problem. Former Finance Minister Jaswant Singh said, it is a lawyer ‘s Budget and not a leader’s. If that is so, the lawyers like Mahatmaji who led the Nation have undoubtedly taken the lead in propelling the country into economic prosperity. The BJP leader’s first reaction was that it is inflationary. But, on the contrary, inflation came down below five per cent immediately a week after the presentation of the Budget. The main Opposition said, the Budget would reverse the economic growth. But, the stock market is booming and there is business confidence all over. So, one can understand their dilemma. Last year, the nation faced deficient monsoon and the unprecedented tsunami disaster. But the country posted with the growth rate of 6.9 per cent GDP. Industrial production was up by 8.4 per cent and exports over 23 per cent. The investment momentum was kept up. Foreign Exchange Reserves crossed 1.2 billion dollars. These are achievements of no means. The country is certainly in the safe hands of intrepid leaders – Congress President and UPA Chairperson Madam Sonia Gandhi, the Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh and the Finance Minister, Mr. P. Chidambaram. The high point of this Budget is the massive investment for social 

* Speech was laid on the Table.

sector. The allocation to health sector has been hiked by over 30 per cent. The farmers will get 30 per cent credit more than last year’s disbursement. It will work out to 1,40,000 crore rupees. Fifty lakh more farmers will be added to the profolio of banks to take them out of the money lenders’ clutches. Rural development will get over Rs. 22,682 crore. The Elementary Education 10,166 crore rupees. Non-rural Roads and Urban Infrastructure 14,896 crore rupees. Urban employed 1,772 crore rupees. Area development, agricultural market, power all put together, the National Commission Minimum Programme will get over 74,849 crore rupees. This works out to 25,000 crore rupees additional allocation for CMP related programmes. Textiles are in a very buoyant mood. Additional 30,000 crore rupees will be invested next year besides 20,000 invested this year. There will be more money in the hands of the people of increase their purchasing power. Another major attempt would be ‘Bharat Nirman’, a project of tall order. It would require 75,000 crore rupees a year for the next 3 years to revamp the entire rural sector – roads, drinking water and all other facilities. No doubt, it is a dream Budget of the rural as well as urban India.

One of the major initiatives is the reform of the Direct Taxes. The Finance Minister has promised to bring forward a brand new Income Tax law by the end of this year. This could be another landmark in the reform process. The peak custom duty has also come down to fifteen per cent. The objective has been ‘lower the tax, higher the compliance’. 

Removal of the excise duty levied by the erstwhile BJP Government on refined edible oil and vanaspathy, which are essential products of daily use by the common man and reverted them back to the exempted list, which would activate price reduction and motivate their production growth in the country. The removal of exemptions under 80-L will hit senior citizens badly. With increasing medi�cal bills every year and decreasing return for their deposits, it would be reasonable to increase the Income Tax exemption limits to two lakhs for a years with savings upto one lakh. Sir, is it necessary tchange at the rate of Rs. 10 for Rs. 10,000 withdrawal of one’s taxed and accounted money? I suggest that this should be abolished and some other alternative measure may be found to check and track large cash withdrawals for black money transactions. If the Finance Minister is very particular about imposing the tax, the threshold limit may be raised to Rs. 1 lakh and cash withdrawals for reasonable expenses like taxes salaries, transport freights may be exempted. 

As we all know, Tsunami was a terrific tragedy of mankind which have swallowed everything from poor fishing community. The nation appreciates with gratitude for the sympathetic response of Madam Soniaji and our Prime Minister. Sir, the life loss is 10273, house loss is 2,39,024, again law loss is 22750. Hence the total loss is 83788.

Though the Central Government has extended all helps and released enough funds. I am sorry the Government of Tamil Nadu is still delaying in extending financial assistance to the affected people stating that they have not yet received guidelines and instructions from the Government of India. The poor fishing community who have lost everything in their life deserve to be helped in all ways without any more delay. I urge upon the Central Government to appoint a Committee consisting of Members of Parliament, to monitor the relief work. 

Regarding, Fringe Benefit Tax, I would like to say that :

This is a welcoming proposal.

A threshold limit may be fixed for the taxable fringe benefit at Rs.1,00,000/- at par with the income tax limit.

The fringe benefit tax paid is not deducted as expense, which should be allowed to be deducted as expense by the employer.

Some reasonable expenses like deepawali gifts to employees, scholarships to the children of the employees and employee welfare expenses shall be exempted. This inclusion will weaken the employer and employee relationship.

Sir, with these views, I conclude my speech.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA (PANSKURA): Sir, I had talked to the hon. Speaker.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : He was kind enough to tell me that I can have my full time.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : Sir, we are discussing the Union Budget of 2005-2006. I appreciate the difficulties of the hon. Finance Minister. Since the Congress could not come to power alone, a combination of political forces is there at place. Contradictory political views and conflicting ideas might have baffled the hon. Finance Minister. Therefore, the present Budget is what it is. In my opinion, the contradictions and conflicts are reflected in the Budget. The Budget is, in my opinion, an unusual product mix. The heart of the Minister is there in the right place, but his hands have been moving in a different direction. There should have been more synchronization between what he feels and what he does. 

Sir, I have no hesitation in appreciating the hon. Finance Minister’s move to introduce Food-For-Work Scheme in 150 districts. Also, I have no hesitation in appreciating the Employment Guarantee Scheme. This is for the first time in India after Independence that the Government is speaking of 100 days employment for one person per family. Never before, however pious might have been the intention, it was never made to be a part of the Budget. I welcome his move for separate allocation for the backward areas, his separate fund for rural development. I should say that I am really touched by his decision to set up 1,88,000 Child Care Centres, ICDS Centres throughout the country. 

The slogan of Bharat Nirman is also unique. Please do not speak of poverty because under the rule of the earlier Government, poverty had accentuated. Better late than never. While sitting on the other side, they did not realise the problem of the people. 

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Shri Gurudas Dasgupta, please address the Chair.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : Sir, I am addressing you. I am only looking at a different direction. Should I look at you?

Now being voted out of power and coming back to Opposition, they might have realised the problem of the poor. While complimenting the hon. Finance Minister for making handsome investments for the social security sector, I have to say, with all humility, that the Budget has not evoked enthusiasm among the common masses from whom the Parliament and the Government derive its power.

Expectations of the people have not been roused. Of course, the stock market is booming. It is on the point of crossing 7,000 point. Never before in the history of free India, the Sensex has been so up-pitched. It is also true that the foreign exchange reserve of the country is excellent. I must say excellent. In one month – in the month of February – there have been inflow of 8 billion American dollars. Thanks to the generous concessions being dolled out by the Government! Sir, I may humbly and frankly submit that, as a party in support of the Government, we have a basic difference with the Budget. The Standing Committee on Finance, constituting Members of different political parties, had unanimously suggested that the direct tax base should broaden. There should be more domestic resources. We need more domestic resources to generate employment, to create houses, to eradicate poverty, to find shelter and to give a better life to the common people of the country.

The important point is that the reforms have benefited the rich undoubtedly. Prof. Abhijit Banerjee, known for his fame in economics, conducted a survey. Apart from that, according to the estimates made by the foreign agencies, India’s position is eighth in the billionaires’ club of the world. How is the wealth measured? Was it not the task of the hon. Minister of Finance to correct this grave anomaly in the social and economic system of the country? I am not speaking about politics; I am speaking about economic equity, social equity and economic balance in the country. Was it not the task of the new Minister of Finance, having the opportunity of preparing a full-fledged Budget, to seek to correct this anomaly? This is one side of the picture.

India’s glorious entry into the billionaires’ club and a billionaire having nine million times more wealth than the GDP is one side of the picture but the other side is more shameful. The per capita availability of food in India is at the standard that was there during World War II. During 1980 the per capita 

availability of food increased. It became 178 kilograms in 1980. Today, it has again gone down to 155 kilograms. There is a massive accumulation of food grains, for which the Government takes credit. The Government believes that if there is a catastrophe in agriculture, India would not be in a grim difficulty because we have enough food.

Why is this massive accumulation of food grains in the country? It is a bane due to lack of purchasing power of a few sections of the people. On the one side, we have a Billionaires’ Club and, on the other side, there is a lack of purchasing power of the downtrodden, leading to accumulation of food grains in the FCI godowns. This is the social anomaly, this is the contradiction, this is the conflict, this is the anachronism and this is the problem of the plenty for the few and poverty for the multitude. Was it not expected that this anomaly would be sought to be corrected? 

I do not believe that one Minister of Finance can correct it. Was it not proper to expect that the corrective step in that direction will be initiated by the Budget in 2005-06? That is not all. Now, let us take the Human Development Index. There is a more telling figure. India occupies 127th place among the comity of nations. It is one of the greatest countries in the world and it is one of the ancient civilisations. This country has been relegated to 127th position in the Human Development Index of the world. 

In the gender equality, we had a most powerful woman Prime Minister of the country. We are proud of her. Today, we have also, if not equally powerful, a powerful lady in the combination of political forces of the country. India produced great eminent women leaders. What about the gender development index? In the gender development index, India’s number is 104. We have a vulgar display of wealth in the country. The most important issue before this country is agriculture. Punjab, the State from where I come, is considered to be a very prosperous State, is considered to be one of the most advanced States in agriculture, and the Punjab farmers are considered to be the most progressive farmers. That is the reason why, today, thousands of farmers are sitting outside the Parliament House protesting against the policies of the Government of India.

To make agriculture economically viable, either the costs of inputs have to be controlled or the prices of agricultural products have to be set at such reasonable prices which give some profit to the farmers. However, over the years, what has been happening is that the prices of inputs have drastically been increasing, whereas the prices of agricultural produce are not increasing at the rate at which they should be increasing. The basic input that a farmer needs is diesel; the basic input that a farmer needs is agricultural labour, implements and credit. 

I will just give you an example. Please look at this one item, diesel. As of 1st January, 2002, the rate of diesel was Rs. 16.28, but today, the rate is diesel is Rs. 25.25. There is a 50 per cent increase in the rate, but the prices of agricultural products have not been increased at that rate.

Another big issue is to make the whole thing economically viable. I have some suggestions to make. The first suggestion I make is that diesel prices should be controlled. We have to subsidise the diesel prices, which is a major input. Otherwise, farming will become economically unviable.

The second major issue which the farmers of Punjab and the farmers around the country are concerned about is the need for funds. What options do they have? One option is to go a moneylender, and the second option is to go to a bank. A moneylender charges more than two per cent per month; sometimes, two-and-a-half per cent per month; and banks’ are charging around 11 per cent. Let us now compare this rate with the rate that it charges for providing funds to other sectors. If you want to buy a tractor, the bank gives you a loan, but it charges 11 per cent or 12 per cent interest and it depends on the loan amount. If a person wants to buy a luxury car, he has just to pay seven per cent or even less than seven per cent. If the industrialists want to take a loan from a bank, he gets the money at eight per cent, nine per cent or 10 per cent interest. This is a major discrimination against the farming community

They do not want to cultivate cotton again. They are planning to switch back to their traditional cropping pattern of wheat and rice next year. 

The second very important issue which I would like to raise is, there has been a continuous discrimination by Government of India against the industries in Punjab. Punjab is a land-locked State. On one side is Pakistan, on top is Jammu and Kashmir, and on the other sides we have Himachal Pradesh, Uttaranchal and Haryana. Any industrialist in the country today, or any multinational company that wants to set up a project in this region, does not come to Punjab. Why? Same is the case in Jammu and Kashmir. You do not have to pay any income tax there. There is no sales tax. Same is the case in Uttaranchal. You do not have to pay any income tax or sales tax. Industrialists of Punjab are dismantling their units, moving their equipment and setting up projects in Himachal, in Uttaranchal. I have paper clippings with me. Everyday it comes in the newspapers. Punjab, as you are aware, is a border State. We have just come out of a very bad patch. You are aware of the fact that for a couple of years there was militancy problem and peace was disturbed. The main cause of it was unemployment. Pakistan took advantage of this unemployment and encouraged disturbance in Punjab. The brave people of Punjab managed to restore peace and get back Punjab. They want Punjab to progress. Punjab is surrounded by all these States which have been given all these incentives. So, I request the hon. Prime Minister that in the national interest all incentives given to the adjacent States be given to Punjab. Punjab also went through the same phase. Punjab also suffered. If that does not happen, industries will start moving out. The hon. Finance Minister was saying that we need a seven or eight or nine per cent growth rate. We want foreign investment; we want people to come to India. The biggest problem that the people are facing today is that there are no rooms available in the hotels in the country. There are only 90,000 rooms in this country. If we want to increase the tourists inflow from three million to six million, we need to create more rooms. We need another minimum one lakh rooms to be added to this industry. If we want to add one lakh rooms, we need Rs.80,000 crore. I am aware of the fact that the Government of India cannot give Rs.80,000 crore. We have to encourage private sector. I personally feel that tourism is actually an infrastructure. I personally request the hon. Finance Minister that hotel industry should get full infrastructure benefits of sales tax and income-tax holiday for a minimum of five to seven years so that they get more inflow of funds, which could be generated to set up new projects to increase their capacity. We would like to request that the Budget allocation to the Ministry of Tourism should at least be doubled so that the Ministry has sufficient funds to promote India worldwide. 

Another thing which I personally want to suggest to the hon. Finance Minister is that we should identify sectors and give special packages to sectors like Buddhist sector which is in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. As you are aware of the fact, South-East Asia has the maximum Buddhist population. 

We should concentrate on this sector by giving special incentives so that people can set up hotels and other infrastructure.

There is another very important sector, the Amritsar Golden Temple. I was watching the other day the BBC Programme on TV. They had conducted a survey on world tourism spots. I was very happy to know that the Golden Temple of Amritsar came as the seventh most favoured destinations of world tourism. I feel that there is very little or no infrastructure available there. The Government of India should come out with a policy for giving special package to Amritsar, the holy city, so that industrialists, hoteliers and other companies can set up projects there.

Another suggestion about the tourism sector is this. The rate of interest charged from the industry should be lowered as it is charged from the infrastructure sector. 

The last area I would like to concentrate on is sports. Fifty per cent of our population consists of youngsters. Whenever Olympic games take place, whenever Asian Games take place or whenever the Commonwealth Games take place, we get depressed by seeing the results. We start blaming our poor athletes. We start blaming our coaches. The blame should go to the Government of India. It is the Government of India which is responsible for the situation that we are in. I was going through the Budget allocation for sports. In the year 2003, it was Rs.385 crore and this year the allocation is Rs.500 crore. Do you thi we can compete worldwide with just Rs.500 crore allocation? If we really want to make a name and if the Government feels that they do not have much funds, then I personally request the hon. Finance Minister to encourage the private sector to come and do it. We should encourage private sector to invest in sports infrastructure. In the case of R&D, companies are given income-tax breaks. They are encouraged by giving 150 per cent income-tax breaks. Similarly, if any company invests in sports infrastructure, it should also be given 150 per cent infrastructure break. Secondly, the Government of India should double the allocation for sports by increasing it up to Rs.1,000 crore.

In the end, on behalf of my party, we do not support this Budget because we personally feel that this Budget is anti-farmers, it is anti-Punjab industry and against the interest of the youth and the common man. I am sure, the suggestions given by us and by my colleagues in the NDA will be considered by the hon. Finance Minister.

*DR. SEBASTIAN PAUL (ERNAKULAM): Sir, the second Budget of the UPA Government is clearly a sunshine Budget. Sunshine after a long winter brings forth hope and expectations. It is creditable on the part of the Finance Minister that he seems to have met them in a fair measure without deviating from the accepted path of the national common minimum programme. The Government is showing willingness to launch a direct action to redress mass poverty and deprivation but unless the problems of illiteracy, ill health and unemployment are addressed properly, it would end as a quixotic exercise. The Finance Minister’s attempt to meet more of the expectations in the social sector through substantial increase in the outlays for employment, education, and health is to be welcomed in this context. The national rural employment guarantee scheme was the most far-reaching of the programmes offered by the UPA in its national common minimum programme. In a Budget that is hailed as a new deal for rural India, Shri Chidambaram has not forgotten this. It is to the credit of the Finance Minister that he could allot higher funding for critical areas of human development including basic education, health, sanitation, housing and rural water supply. Let us wish that Shri Chidambaram’s unexpected departure from expected targets would not frustrate his attempt to reach deficit reduction targets. Binding deficit reduction goals is a restraint and within it the Finance Minister has done a commendable job. I support him in that noble endeavour.

* I want to congratulate the present Government for taking a balanced approach towards the development of Developed States and backward States. Developed States are not penalised at the cost of Backward States. Social security should be provided to the economically weaker sections also by way of providing pension, educational loans etc. Non-plan expenditure is increasing. This should be curbed and suitable steps should be taken towards this.

Pension reforms should be carried out with rational approach within the next four years, else the pension bill will soar and will be uncontrollable.

Water resources: There are problems between the states on the issue of sharing of water of the rivers flowing through them. We can initiate a scheme in which the water within the State is circulated from surplus area to deficient area to reduce the water shortage (Intra-linking of Rivers). Moreover, the water from surplus area to deficient area may transported, like in Maharashtra the Godavari and Tapi basins are deficient and the surplus water from Konkan rivers can be transported to these basins. After the water requirement of the State is satisfied after intra-linking, the remaining surplus water should be transported to the deficient states, because in the coming years shortage of water will be huge as the population is exploding and this will give rise to social tensions. We should give a serious thought to this scheme. The Maharashtra Pani Parishad took the initiative and formulated such scheme and submitted it to the Government of Maharashtra which has already such proposal of intra-linking of rivers when the Central Government initiated such policy in 2002. More than 50 per cent of Maharashtra is under drought as per the Government of India norms and the Government has already classified Maharashtra as water scarce region. 

*Speech was laid on the Table.

Rural Development and Wastelands: The big builders and construction lobby has been converting fertile and irrigated land around the cities for the purpose of developing residential and commercial complexes. The Government has invested huge amounts of public money, almost Rs.1000 crore in the last five years to develop the wastelands and make them cultivable and creation of infrastructure like roads, drinking water, irrigation. Moreover, there also has been huge private investment on these lands. These funds are nothing but waste if the builder lobby exploits such land. This is totally un-understandable proposition. Due to this the agricultural land is becoming scarce thereby putting more stress on the already stressed available cultivable land. The builder lobby industrialists should be allowed to develop on the wastelands and the funds for this purpose can be utilised for other social sectors. Industrial land must be saved, as it is a major employment provider in rural areas.

I would like to suggest here that looking at the seriousness of this problem, the urban areas may be allowed to grow vertically, by providing more FSI and the funds thus saved can be used for providing better urban amenities and infrastructure. 

Drinking water is another problem area. So far, 95 per cent of the habitats are being completely provided with drinking water. 4.6 per cent of the localities are partially covered and 0.4 per cent are still yet to be covered. It is the most unfortunate thing that after 57 years of independence the Government is unable to provide basic amenities. This programme should be vigorously pursued by providing more funds. The localities covered are also in a bad shape as the components are ill maintained, not functioning properly.Rain Water Conservation and Sand Bed: I would also like to draw the attention to the problem of exploiting sand from the riverbeds for the use of construction activities. Sand is the natural water reservoir. I have taken up this matter with the Government of Maharashtra, which has realized the gravity of this problem and issued a ban on such exploitation. Alternative to sand should be identified and introduced. Appropriate amount should be provided in the Budget for purpose of research and incentive should be given for the use of such product in the construction and road projects. No mention and provision for Rain-water Harvesting scheme in this Budget. In order to enurage the rainwater conservation the sand beds are the natural medium. Unreasonable exploitation has lead to depletion of the water bodies and ground water levels. An integrated approach should be followed and use of locally conserved water should be encouraged so that the cost of water transportation can be minimised. 

Education & Skill Development Initiative: The Human resource base of India is its greatest asset with over 50 per cent of the population under the age of 25 and with ageing in the other countries, such as 38 in Europe and 41 in Japan and 30 in China. In 2025, India will have a dependency ratio of 12.1 for every 100 working adults. There will be slightly more than 12 persons who would be above the age of 65. For China the ratio will be 19.4, for Japan it is 49 and for Europe it is 33.2. Clearly India enjoys the advantage, which can be converted into an opportunity for national well being, by making India the Skill Capital of the World. To achieve this objective, we should ramp up private sector initiative and skill our human resource to globally benchmarked standards, thus enhancing our per capita productivity across all sectors of our economy and put India on the glide path for all round sustainable development. 

The scheme is already operational as a pilot project at Pravaranagar, District Ahmednagar, Maharashtra, Shillong (North-East) and Baramulla (J&K). It is being executed at a minimal cost of Rs.5000 per child spread over 100-200 hours training periods depending upon the type of skill being imparted. 

Sarva Shikshan Abhiyan: It is a novel scheme but lacks the local component. *SHRI D NARBULA (DARJEELING): I support the General Budget presented by Hon’ble Finance Minister, Shri Chidambaram for the year 2005-06.

At the very outset, I compliment the Hon’ble Finance Minister for this pro-people Budget. It was beyond anybody’s imagination that the Tax brackets could be raised to Rs. 1 lakh and Rs. 1.25 lakh for women and Rs. 1.5 lakh for senior citizens. This will not only benefit a large number of middle income group of people but also more people will come forward to file their annual income returns.

The Hon’ble Finance Minister has promised that Education Loan would be given liberally to the students. 1,40,000 loans amounting to Rs. 2,249 crores have been given up to 31st December, 2004.

Under Antyogaya Anna Yojana, 2 crore families will be benefited. The UPA Government now proposes to increase the number of family to 2.5 crores in the year 2005-06.

The children of Lower Middle Class and Middle Class Income Group go to schools where Mid Day Meal is being provided under the Mid Day Meal Scheme. Eleven crores children are benefited under this scheme today. The UPA Government is now providing the cost of foodgrain as well as the conversion cost. The allocation for the next year is proposed to be increased to Rs. 3.010 crores. 

Here I would like to draw attention of the Government that the money provided under this scheme in many cases is not used properly. Rampant corruption is there between authorities and contractors who are entrusted with the job to provide food to the children. I suggest that the Government should be vigilant so that this scheme is properly implemented and the children are fully benefited.

Under the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan, the UPA Government has allocated Rs. 3057 crores last year and Government has enhanced the allocation to Rs. 4754 crores during this year. This scheme helps to decrease the number of drop outs in

* Speech was laid on the Table.

the School. The Government is also considering punishment for parents who prevent their children from going to primary schools.

"Prarambhik Siksha Kosh" has been created for funding this programme and the Hon. Finance Minister has proposed to increase the allocation to Rs. 7156 crores in 2005-06.

The UPA Government has taken a special care of SC/ST students by providing them scholarship that will meet the requirements for their tuition fees, living expenses, books and a computer.

These scholarships will be given to those SC/ST students who get admission in one of the institutes of excellence, notified by the Government.

During the current year, 31355 rural habitations have been provided drinking water facilities under Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking water Mission. During the year 2005-06, more habitations will be covered and impasses will be given to improve the drinking water quality in about 2.16 lacs in Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Rajasthan, West Begal and other States. The Hon’ble Finance Minister proposes to increase the outlay for the mission to the tune of Rs. 4750 crores in the next year. In the matter of Drinking water, the constituency that I hail is having a great crisis of drinking water through Darjeeling has monsson for about 6 months in a year the people of this district have been suffering from acute shortage of drinking water since last 50 years. The UPA Government has now taken up the initiative to solve this problem of my constituency. The Hon. Minister of Water Resources has already sent a proposal approved by the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council to Government of West Bengal for its approval and once it is approved I request the Hon. Finance Minister to allocate the money during this financial year for the implementation of the said scheme and help to solve the long standing problem of the people of my constituency.

UPA Government has also given attention for providing sanitation facilities in the rural household, a total sanitation campaign now operates in 452 districts and the Government now intends to extend the total sanitation campaign to all districts and proposes to allocate these 630 crores for the next year. While 

welcoming this decision, I would urge upon the Government to ensure proper and timely implementation of the programme in rural and backward districts of the country like Darjeeling.

The UPA Government has also realized the difficulties faced by the plantation sector. The Government has set up an expert committee to suggest improvement in this sector. The tea industry has been facing difficulties because of the declining of productivity of tea. The Government is now examining way and means of introducing a programme for massive implementation and rejuvenation. My constituency is surrounded by tea gardens. A good amount of export quality tea which fetches good amount of foreign exchange by exporting Darjeeling tea but surcharge of Re. 1 per k.g. was a big burden. I compliment to the Hon’ble Finance Minister for his proposal to abolish the surcharge which helps to minimize the cost of production and it will bring a big relief to improve the present position of tea industry and also provide relief to the poor working class people who earn their livelihood by plucking green leaf.

I also congratulate to the Hon’ble Finance Minster for his proposal to abolish the excise duty of Re. 1/- per k.g. on refined edible oil and Rs. 1.25 per k.g. on vanaspati. The Hon’ble Finance Minister also proposed to remove the custom duty on LPG for domestic consumption and substitute kerosene where excise duty will also be nil. This will bring a great relief to the people of lower income group.

The UPA Government has given a great relief to the people of the middle and lower income group of country and, therefore, it is a pro-people Budget and therefore, I support this pro-people Budget for the year 2005-06 and once again congratulate the Hon’ble Finance Minister and Hon’ble Prime Minister of India and Smt. Sonia Gandhi and Chairperson of UPA.

MR. CHAIRMAN : Next, Shri K. Yerrannaidu – absent.

Shri Rajesh Verma.

*SHRI ABDUL RASHID SHAHEEN (BARAMULLA): In October 1996, the Prime Minister made an announcement of "New initiatives for North Eastern Region" and announced that at least 10 per cent of the Budget of the Central Ministries/Departments will be spent in North Eastern States for their development.

Then the exercise of Planning Commission in consultation with Ministries and Central Departments revealed that the initiative fell short of the stipulated target of 10 per cent spending. The exercise was made during 1997-98 and, therefore, the Central Government created a Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) for the North East out of the unspent amount of stipulated 10 per cent GBS for upgrading and supporting the infrastructure development projects in North East. This has been the position right from 1996.

We are happy and wish North East well. We understand the shortage of resources and poor infrastructure keep breeding unemployment and hence the resentment and discontent among the people of such area, ultimately culminates into violence and sometimes into bloody feuds as in some of the North East States and Kashmir. But, we have had urged upon the Government, time and again, that J&K should have been included in the arrangements like this. At least 5 per cent of the budgetary allocations, if not more, could have been addressed to the most of the problems of the State. Infrastructure development could have set the stage for a bigger leap in the economic activity in Jammu and Kashmir.

The above mentioned arrangement, that is, connecting to NLCPR, could have given an assured roadmap towards development and eradication of unemployment in the J&K, particularly to Kashmir which has been emaciated by the militancy and continued economic disaster for more than a decade.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

When we raise this issue, we are being given assurance of packages. When PM’s package is announced, the whole country comes to believe that Kashmir is a big drain on the economy of India.

Hon. Finance Minister has announced that the current plan shall be fixed at Rs. 4200 crore instead of Rs. 3008 crore and Baghihar shall be provided adequate funds next year.

Hon. Finance Minister has also been kind to mention that Udhampur-Baramulla Rail project shall be treated as a ‘Project of National Importance’.

We are highly thankful for making a mention of Jammu & Kashmir in the Budget speech. But, I would like to know, Sir, that what is the ‘reconstruction plan’ and what exactly shall be expenditure allocated for such reconstruction plan.

And also we are expecting to know that why Kashmir can’t be included in the Scheme of NLCPR. Hon. Finance Minister has pleaded the cause of the poor and I quote from his speech "Government holds that its sacred duty is to empower the poor and eliminate the scourge of poverty". 

We appreciate the intention and indepth feeling of the Government about eliminating poverty. That is why we expect from the Government that our demand for linking us (Kashmir) to NLCR shall be considered and announcement to this effect shall be made by the hon. Finance Minister.

Sir, the minority communities constitute 18.42 per cent of the total population of the country. We are aggrieved that in the Budget 2005-06, substantial allocations have not been made for the education and economic development of the minorities. Therefore, in this backdrop, we suggest that Maulana Azad Education Foundation, which was established in the year 1989, was given only one crore in the current financial year. The Foundation activities are sustained on the income generated from the corpus funds of Rs. 70 crore. The Foundation has made considerable contribution since its inception by sanctioning more than Rs. 75 crore to 580 NGO’s by providing grants-in-aid for their establishment and expansion of schools, colleges, residential schools and upgrading existing professional and technical institutes.

As we are aware, the hon. Finance Minister in his Budget speech dated 7th July, 2004, mentioned that additional education cess of two per cent will be laid and estimated income of Rs. 4000 to 5,000 crore will be generated from the education cess. The income received from the education cess will be spent on educational development programmes. In our country, the nodal Ministry of Education is HRD. However, the Ministry of SJ&E is the nodal ministry for SC, OBC, handicapped and minorities. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (SJ&E) has introduced various schemes for these deprived sections of the society. The Maulana Azad Eudcaion Foundation, under the Ministry of SJ&E, is looking after the educational development of the minorities.

So, it shall be highly desired that the hon. Finance Minister announces an allocation of Rs. 200 crore to the Foundation from the amount collected as education cess and Rs. 50 crore be provided for yearly scholarship programme. This positive step can generate the education programme in the minority community and that will be a gesture of justice towards the depressed sections of the minorities.

Sir, in the Budget of 2005-06, the Government proposes to increase the equity support to NMDFC. We request that the equity for the NMDFC be enhanced to at least Rs. 300 crore. It is also surprising to note that, despite the Government’s promise to increase the equity, the Budgetary documents (Expenditure Budget 2005-06 Volume I) page 41 shows that for 2005-06, the Budget allocation is only Rs. 19.60 crore. Whereas, for this financial year, it was Rs. 71.29 crore. The same is also shown in expenditure Budget (2005-06) Vol. II at page 190.

The other important point, which deserves the attention of the UPA Government is that the Government proposes to give a certain percentage of new schools under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan as well as the Kasturba Balika Vidhyalaya Scheme. We propose that 18.42 per cent should be given to the minorities under the above mentioned schemes as per their population. The Government’s decision to provide central assistance for recruiting and posting of Urdu-language teachers is commendable and welcome step.

To conclude, I will again remind the hon. Finance Minister that unemployed youths are waiting with a big hope that the promise of the Government that the "opportunity to learn a skill and be gainfully employed" shall be fulfilled in their case on priority".

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA (SAMBALPUR): Thank you Mr. Chairman, Sir. I will try to be very precise and try to give my opinions point-wise. Therefore, my humble request is – do not ring your bell to test my nerve. I am a bit nervous fellow. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : If you confine your observations within time, I have no objection. 

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : I will do it. 

My friend, Shri Kharabela Swain was telling that Shri Chidambaram is the luckiest Finance Minister of this country. While agreeing with Shri Swain, I also compliment the hon. Minister of Finance for being the luckiest Finance Minister of this country because he has presented a Budget on a very comfortable economic backdrop, a very comfortable growth including growth of manufacturing sector. Therefore, the hon. Minister of Finance should be grateful to the NDA which through prudence and wisdom brought stability and growth to the economy of this country. 

I was going through many of the announcements in the Budget by the hon. Minister of Finance and I was surprised to mark the similarity in many of the projects. Many of the schemes which were initiated during the NDA regime have just been renamed. The nomenclatures were changed. He would give different names to the NDA programmes to take credit for innovation. Connecting Rashtriya Shram Vikas Yojana to Backward Region Development Fund and Food for Work programme to National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme or calling sprinkle irrigation as micro irrigation is no new innovation. Concepts like viability gap funding of infrastructure, a fund for medium and small enterprises, emphasis on diversion of agriculture and value addition agro processing and agro-export, provision of urban facilities in rural areas etc. were initiated by NDA Government. Therefore, the hon. Minister of Finance ought to be grateful to the NDA Government. 

In the print media as well as in the electronic media, the hon. Minister of Finance has been projected and this Budget is being projected as a dream Budget. 

Indeed, I want that it should be a dream Budget. … (Interruptions) No, it is not a real Budget. Immediately after the presentation of the Budget, the off-hand reaction was very favourable. It was appreciated by everybody - by the media, by the common man. After one or two days when people got time to go through the fine print, the reality was exposed. Many segments of the society including the industry, the trade, the taxation experts, the academicians, civil society, and I should say, even the partners of UPA including the Left have severely criticised this Budget. 

In this Budget, the Finance Minister has tried to appease all sections of the society. The Finance Minister has also attempted to please all including the multinationals and the corporate sector. He has tried to please the salaried class; he has also tried to please the farmer by enhancing the credit flow by 30 per cent in the next year; he also tried to, of course, appease the working women including the housewives; he has tried to appease the poor; and not the least, he has tried his utmost to please the champions of the poor sitting here. Sir, this is his compulsion.

Let me come to the point of fiscal deficit. The Finance Minister promises to keep the deficit under check by off-loading budgetary expenditure. Rs. 29,000 crore of Central loans for State Plans have been off-loaded on the States and they are supposed to borrow money from the markets. If it were retained in the Central Budget, the fiscal deficit would be 5.1 per cent instead of 4.3 per cent, as indicated. In effect, the Central deficit has been converted into a State deficit. The combined fiscal deficit of Centre and States taken together has reached an alarming level of ten per cent.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : Sir, it is no consolation for the Central Government to decrease its own deficit at the States'''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''' expenses. The Finance Minister says that he has done this juggling on the recommendations of the Twelfth Finance Commission. As I have understood - I may be wrong because I am not an expert in economics - the Twelfth Finance Commission had given the option to States to finance Plan expenditure through market borrowings instead of borrowing from the Central Government. Many poorer States like Orissa, which are already in a debt trap, may not be able to access market loans. As such, to deny them access to Central loans may amount to cutting State Plan outlays, which is indeed very unfortunate. 

Sir, for the national Food for Work Programme or National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, 50 lakh metric tonnes of food grains have been provided. There is no mention about its funding in the Budget. Obviously, it means that the Food Corporation of India will lend it to the Central Government. This is a strange budgetary exercise. 

Again, Rs. 10,000 crore for infrastructure development are also off- Budget. It will be raised by Special Purpose Vehicle, PSV, through local or foreign currency sources. This kind of budgetary juggling is not a healthy trend and these off-Budget expenditures may escape, I fear, the scrutiny of this Parliament also. 

Much emphasis has been given in the Budget to rural development. Sir, I compliment hon. Finance Minister for this. Budget contribution to Central Plan under rural development is Rs. 11,494 crore while BE for 2003-04 was Rs. 11,939 crore. The Budget Estimate (BE) for 2003-2004 was Rs. 11,369 crore. The same level has been maintained, and it is mentioned that they are giving much emphasis on rural development.

The Finance Minister has spun a web of dreams like a dream merchant, but without adequate budgetary provisions to turn his dreams into reality. So, I think, this Budget is not a dream Budget, but he is a daydreamer.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please be precise.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : The Common Minimum Programme (CMP) talks about 2 per cent to 3 per cent of GDP to be spent on health. The requirement for the same is Rs. 70,000 crore. The Finance Minister has increased the allocation for it from Rs. 8,420 crore to Rs. 10,280 crore. How many years will this Government take to reach their CMP goal with this meagre allocation?

Similarly, for education, the CMP envisaged to get 6 per cent of the GDP, but the present increase falls short of this ambitious goal.

As regards irrigation and flood control, the increase is meagre, that is, Rs. 443 crore over last year. Last year also an increase of only Rs. 15 crore have been provided. How does the Government think of improving the irrigation facilities for the farmers with this meagre allocation?

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please conclude your speech.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : Sir, please give me a couple of minutes more to speak. The Finance Minister has very conveniently forgotten about the issue of disinvestment. What is the stand of the present Government on the issue of disinvestment? I would like to know categorically about it from the hon. Finance Minister.

The backbone of this Government, and the Finance Minister is bent heavily because their backbone is here, and without their support they cannot continue in the Government.

The Finance Minister has envisaged increasing the credit flow for the farmers by 30 per cent in the next year. It is no doubt a welcome proposition, but I am afraid that the Finance Minister has very conveniently forgotten about the high rate of interest charged to the farmers. We have to be very considerate about the policy for the farmers to repay the loan. At this high rate of interest being charged from the farmers we cannot prevent them from committing suicide. We have to be very careful about the capability of the farmers in repaying the loan.

15.43 hrs. (Dr. Laxminarayan Pandey in the Chair) 

Only extending a higher percentage of the loan to the farmers is not enough. We must take necessary steps to see that the capability of the farmers is enhanced, and they are in a position to repay the loan.

As regards the Crop Insurance Policy also there has been a request, and a demand from all sections that there should be changes in the Crop Insurance Policy. The Gram Panchayat should be treated as the unit to assess the crop loss, instead of tehsils. This would provide better facilities to the farmers. But the Finance Minister has not mentioned anything about the change of policy in the Crop Insurance Scheme. 

I would urge upon the Finance Minister that during his reply he should very categorically point out the stand of the Government on this issue. I am saying this because thousands of farmers are waiting for this.

MR. CHAIRMAN : Please conclude your speech.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : Sir, just give me two more minutes to speak. I would come to another very important point. I was surprised when Mr. Gurudas Dasgupta was very eloquently and sharply attacking this Government. Their party is a part and parcel of this Government.

The hon. Finance Minister has forgot about the defaulters in this country. I have read a report from a newspaper on this issue. I am not sure whether it is correct or not. The report says that, today, the NPA had totaled to Rs. 15,00,000 crore in this country.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please wind up your speech.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA (SAMBALPUR): This is nothing but loot of the national exchequer. The Government should come out with the list of defaulters, and criminal proceedings should be initiated against them. If a poor farmer takes some loan and is unable to repay the loan in time, then he is subject to all kinds of legal harassment.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Next, Dr. K. S. Manoj.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : Ultimately, he commits suicide, but the big corporate houses and big people in this country are very conveniently escaping from it. 

Sir, I would now come to my last point.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please cooperate with the Chair. I have already called the name of the next speaker.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : I come from a very poor State. I do not object to the Government giving special aid to States like Bihar, etc.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Acharya, you have already taken about 14 minutes. Please conclude your speech.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : My only question to the hon. Finance Minister is, "What is the parameter or the basis on which you decide to give special grants or special packages to States?" Orissa is the poorest of the poor States in the country. Forty-seven per cent of the people are living below the poverty line; the largest percentage of people are living below the poverty line.

MR. CHAIRMAN : Please conclude. Otherwise, I will not allow it to go on record.

SHRI PRASANNA ACHARYA : Orissa, in spite of our requests, has not been granted any special package. I would urge upon the Prime Minister to keep this above politics and consider granting a special package to Orissa.

DR. K.S. MANOJ (ALLEPPEY): Sir, thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to take part in the discussion on the General Budget. 

I rise to support the General Budget presented by the hon. Finance Minister. At the outset, I must congratulate the hon. Minister for keeping the promises that he has made to the common man while presenting the Budget for the year 2004-05. Adequate attention was given to farmers, students, self-employed women and labourers in search of work and food. However, a large number of people working in the field of traditional industries, cottage and small-scale industries have been forgotten by the Government. 

I am happy to note that in the Budget for 2005-06, as suggested by the Left parties, though not fully, the allocation for education, health and family welfare, and rural development has been enhanced. In contrast to globalisation policies, the hon. Finance Minister has maintained the subsidy on fertilisers. In his Budget Speech also, he reiterated that the subsidies would continue. 

I agree with the hon. Finance Minister that India is not a poor country. We have rich resources, heritage, tradition and culture. Yet, a significant portion of our people is poor. We have enough resources and wealth to meet the needs of every citizen, but not enough to meet the greed of even a single person. Some of the reasons why we are failing in meeting the needs of many are improper distribution of resources and wealth, and also due to centralisation of wealth. There is no social equity, economic equity and equity in power. The economic policies that we are following will harm our efforts to bring growth, equity and stability. This economic policy will widen the gap between the haves and the have-nots. 

The National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme and National rural Mission are welcome measures. The Finance Minister has pointed out that the focus of National Rural Health Mission is on strengthening of primary healthcare through interventions based on community ownership. I fear the term ‘community ownership’. I suspect a hidden agenda in this. I fear that it is a move to transfer the responsibility of the State from providing primary healthcare to the shoulders of the citizens, just like what we have done in the field of education. In the field of 

education, formally, it was the duty of the State to provide free and universal education for all. However, now, it has become the responsibility of the parents to give education to their children. Thus, more and more children are missing their opportunity to study. Due to the implementation of this community ownership programme, I fear the responsibility to maintain their health will also

fall on their shoulders. The Finance Minister proposes to double the supplementary nutrition norms. That is a welcome measure. However, the Centre will meet only half the expenditure incurred for this purpose. I would request the hon. Minister to ensure that whatever additional expenditure is incurred for doubling the supplementary nutrition programme be given to the States. Otherwise, the intention will not be fulfilled. I now come to drinking water and sanitation. Availability of pure and safe drinking water has become a serious problem in various parts of the country. Availability of safe drinking water is a problem in Kerala also. However, the State of Kerala is not included under the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission. I, therefore, request the Finance Minister to include Kerala also in the Mission. In the field of investments, opening up of more and more areas in the services sector for to private vestment – both domestic and foreign investment – is not a welcome move. Services sector accounts for about 52 per cent of our GDP. Opening up services sector to private players will only provide scope for looting of our wealth and growth. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : Please conclude now. I have given a lot of time.

DR. K.S. MANOJ : I am concluding, Sir.

Increasing the cess on petrol and diesel by 50 paise per litre, has resulted in the total amount of cess increasing to Rs.1.5 a litre. My humble request to the hon. Finance Minister is that this cess should not be imposed on diesel and kerosene used for fishing vessels and trawlers. If this is imposed on diesel used by fishing sector, the benefit of subsidy that is presently given – of Rs.1.5 a litre - will be nullified. This will be a blow to the fishing industry. 

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please conclude now. 

DR. K.S. MANOJ : Elimination of standard deduction, Section 88B and 80L is actually a blow to the senior citizens. Earlier a pension drawing senior citizen with a gross income of Rs.1,95,880, and other senior citizens with income of Rs.1,53,330 were not required to pay income tax. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : If you do not conclude now, your speech will not go on record. 

DR. K.S. MANOJ : I am concluding, Sir. 

But now they have to pay Rs.9066 and Rs.666 respectively. To lift this curse on the senior citizens, the hon. Minister of Finance should revisit the matter. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : Shri Chinta Mohan. Dr. Manoj, I have called the name of the next speaker.

DR. K.S. MANOJ : Sir, due to paucity of time, I conclude. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : If you want to say something more, you can lay your speech. 

SHRI KINJARAPU YERRANNAIDU (SRIKAKULAM): Sir, we are ready to sit even up to 8 o’clock. Today is the last day and the Finance Minister will reply to the debate. You have to allow all the Members to speak. 

DR. CHINTA MOHAN (TIRUPATI): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to lay my speech on the Table of the House. In addition to that, I would like to make a few points.

Overall Budget is very good. The Finance Minister has put in a lot of hard work to give a very balanced Budget to this country. With all humility, I would request him about the Mid-Day Meal Programme. Under this Programme, he is giving meal to 11 crore children every day in the primary schools. They are giving 100 grams of rice per day per child, which is very little. I would request the hon. Finance Minister that if he can increase it from 100 grams to 150 grams per day per child, 11 crore children will get benefit out of it. 

The conversion charges for this Mid-Day Meal Programme is Re.1 per month per child. Instead of Re.1, I would request him to make it Rs.2 so that it would give better meal to the children.

Under the ICDS Programme, which is a very good and laudable programme, he is helping one crore pregnant women. In addition to one crore pregnant women, if he can add one more crore and increase it to two crores, it will go a long way in helping the poor people. When the other side was ruling, they brought the Antyodaya Scheme on the Christmas Day, 2000. It is a very good programme. Under this Scheme, they are giving 35 kgs. of wheat at the rate of Rs.2 per kg per month. They are also giving Rs. 3 Kilogram rice. If the Scheme is extended little more - Four crore, another 

one and half crore poor people would derive advantage out of if.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: I have already increased it from 2 to 2.5 crores. DR. CHINTA MOHAN : If you can make it to four crores by extending it, they all will have good food. Today, Government is planning to building AIIMS-like hospitals, the temples of health, in different parts of the country. This project should be started quickly so that these would remain temples of health all over the country.Coming to the recruitment, he has said that he is going to create employment opportunities. But in 2001, Shri Yashwant Sinha, the then Finance Minister, has brought recruitment optimisation. Every year, 1.20 lakh employees are retiring from the Central Government. Out of that, on compassionate ounds, they are recruiting 40,000 people, and they are not giving jobs to the balance 80,000. The rule of optimisation should be scrapped. They should go in for full employment because today the educated youth is in frustration; they are taking drugs; they are addicted to drugs; and they are going towards Moaists activists. We have to create hope in these educated unemployed people, who are about four crore. They are all weeping. In the national interest, this rule should be scrapped, which was brought in by the Opposition in 2001. With all humility, I request him to take a view of it and see that this is employment optimization removed.
