*SHRI B. VINOD KUMAR : As a first time MP elected on the regional aspirations of Backward Telangana, on behalf of Telangana Rashtra Samithi, I convey my gratitude to Hon. Finance Minister, Shri P. Chidambaram Garu for devoting almost more than one hour of his Budget speech to the components of National Common Minimum Programme and to outline the Government’s commitment to social sector development and rural India and agriculture. Such a Budget speech with inclusive agenda for development was long overdue and was not heard in this august house of Parliament aftermath of Economic Reforms. The Budget speech in character partly justifies the mandate given by the people of this country to the UPA Alliance.

I always hold that the Reforms initiated in our country since 1991 have been necessary keeping in view of the global trends, but this reform process needs to be continued with social and rural sensitivity to make it sustainable and equitable. On that score, this Budget reflected remarkable social and rural sensitivity in its approach to the issues and allocations. For this, I must congratulate the Hon. Prime Minister, Shri Manmohan Singhji and the Chairperson of UPA Alliance, Smt. Sonia Gandhiji for providing necessary directional inputs in this regard.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

Sir, coming to the specific proposals of the Budget, the increased allocations to health sector by Hon. Finance Minister under National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) from Rs. 8,420 crores to Rs. 10,280 crores and to Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) from 1623 crores to Rs. 3,142 crores need to be applauded. Sir, similar effort by Hon. Finance Minister to increase Budget Allocation to Mid Day Meal Scheme from Rs. 1,675 crore to Rs. 3,010 crore and create a ‘non-lapsable fund called Prarmbhik Shiksha Kosh’ for Sarva Shikshan Abhiyan by increasing allocations to Rs. 7156 crores from Rs.4,754 crores is also equally praiseworthy.

Equally commendable, Sir, is the increased allocations to Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission and Total Sanitation Campaign (TCS) which would positively enhance the quality and dignity of life in our villages.

This Budget was also path-breaking in providing an exclusive statement on the schemes for development of SCs and STs and the respective allocations. It also makes a commitment for inclusive economic growth by involving the SCs/STs in development process. I would request the Hon’ble Finance Minister that Government should release date State-wise and District-wise, with regard to funds utilisation and beneficiaries at half-yearly intervals so as to ensure that his inclusive process in indeed more broad-based.

Another praiseworthy initiative is the announcement of new window of opportunity to SC/ST students for prosecuting higher education in the Institutes of Excellence through provision of large scholarships. I would again request the Hon. Finance Minister to operationalise this Scheme during this academic year itself by giving wide publicity in each District Headquarters. I would also request the Hon’ble Finance Minister to examine the involvement of local Member of Parliament along with District Administration in the selection process of awarding these scholarships. Similarly, an half-yearly report on the progress of implementation of this Scholarship Scheme with District wise beneficiaries may please be submitted to Parliament. I also commend similar procedure of selection, reporting and review for adoption in the proposed Rajiv Gandhi National Fellowship for SC and ST students for pursuing M.Phil and Ph.D. course in selected universities.

Sir, Indian agriculture and farmers are passing through the testing times and Hon. Finance Minister too acknowledged this reality in the Budget speech. Sir, UPA alliance has gained the power at Centre by aggressively articulating the failures of the previous Government in rural and agriculture sector and by raising the aspirations of Indian farmers who constitute 65% of Indian population. Sir, time has now come to redeem our pledge and commitment to Indian farmers in a more demonstrative manner. In this context, I would like to bring to your kind attention, Sir, that the Finance Minister himself admitted in a Press Conference at Hyderabad that only four crores of farmers out of 11.55 crores of farmers in the country have access to institutionalised credit. Majority of them farmers in the country numbering around 9.27 crores are small and marginal farmers. This is dismal and unacceptable situation and calls for urgent measures/steps on ‘war-footing’ to provide institutionalised credit to these 11.55 crore farmers within a period of two to three years. But, Speaker, Sir, the Finance Minister’s initiatives and the performances figures with regard to provision of rural credit and indebtedness leave much to be desired Sir, there is no reflection of urgency and bold initiatives for rural credit in this Budget, which itself outlined a new deal in many other sectors. The dependence of Finance Minister in capacity of NABARD and RBI for attainment of the rural credit targets as grass-root level is not adequate enough to bridge the gaps in rural credit expeditiously. The hon. Finance Minister mentioned about the acceptance of the recommendations and report of Task Force on Rural Co-operative Baking in principle and involving the State Governments in consultative process. This process of restructuring of Cooperatives has been hanging on fire for more than a decade and a lasting solution is still evading. Involving the State Governments for consultative process and restructuring these cooperatives would stretch beyond the term of this 14th Lok Sabha. The extension of credit to 58.5 lakh farmers in current year and the proposed target of 50 lakh new farmers in the next years are far far below the potential rural credit gap to 7.55 crore farmers who are yet to be credit-linked. Therefore, Speaker, Sir, I would like to request Hon’ble Finance Minister to examine the launching a "National Rural Credit Mission" to ensure the rural credit to all eligible farmers within next three years. This missionary approach calls for total restructuring and gearing up of NABARD, Regional rural banks and rural branches of commercial banks which are in control of Central Government. Simultaneously, the Government may continue the efforts of restructuring the Co-operatives through involvement of State Governments. Otherwise, Speaker, Sir, the farming community would be unforgiving if UPA Alliance does not tackle this critical issue with all its energies and capabilities at its disposal. Therefore, I once again humbly request the Hon. Prime Minister and Hon. Chairperson of UPA and Hon. Finance Minister to revisit this critical issue of rural credit and indebtedness with utmost seriousness and concern. Speakers, Sir, similar urgency and seriousness need to be displayed in redesigning the existing Crop Insurance Scheme to make it more transparent and farmer friendly. The Hon. Finance Minister has proposed to extend the present form of Crop Insurance for one year. But, Speaker, Sir, the time is running out and the country’s millions of farmers are eagerly awaiting a totally revamped and user friendly Crop Insurance Scheme. Therefore, Speaker, Sir, I would like to draw kind attention of the Finance Minister that these twin issues of Rural Credit Coverage to all eligible farmers and revamping of Crop Insurance Scheme are going to be the greatest challenge of UPA Alliance and I request Hon. Finance Minister to deal these two issues with same boldness and finesse he displayed in tackling the issue of economic growth and equity. Speaker, Sir, the Finance Minister needs to be complimented for making a bold announcement on Outcome v/s outlay debate. There are no two opinions, Sir, that delivery mechanism and performance of Government would have to be improved substantially to reach the Aam Admi. In this context, I would like to suggest to Finance Minister that, to start with, the district-wise and constituency-wise allocations of Budget outlay for various schemes of Government may please be provided to all Members of Parliament and may also be put on the website of the Government. This would not be asking too much, Sir, considering that we are expecting similar information flow and transparency from Panchayat Raj Institutions at grass root level.

Now, coming to Part B of the Budget speech, Speaker, Sir, I and my party compliment the Finance Minister for his efforts towards rationalisation and simplification of direct tax regime for individual tax payers. I also compliment the Finance Minister for downward revision of customs duties on various items as this would lead to considerable reduction of prices and make these products affordable to Aam Admi.

I welcome the announcements with regard to constitution of Knowledge Commission, National Urban Renewal Mission, Creation of Regional Finance Centre at Mumbai. These are long awaited initiatives which deserve full justification.

Coming to the critical proposal of two anti-tax evasion measures, the logic of Hon. Finance Minister in shaping up these proposals in impeccable. But, Speaker, Sir, I would like to remind Hon. Finance Minister that his noble intentions about movement to Cheque economy are not supported by extant infrastructure relating to Cheque Clearing system in the hinterland of the country. There are many hundreds of emerging towns, where established clearing system is conspicuous by its absence. Under such circumstances of infrastructure deficit, imposing a tax on cash withdrawal of Rs. 10,000/- and above would pose serious and unavoidable hassles to farmers, small businesses, micro-credit players and marginal classes. These small towns do not have the luxury of credit card or debit card infrastructure. Therefore, I request the Finance Minister to remodel the proposal on the basis of availability of Cheque Clearing Infrastructure and fix separate limits for urban/metro and semi-urban/rural branches. The revised limits may be Rs. 50,000/- for rural and semi-urban branches where clearing system is absent and Rs. 20,000/- for metro/urban branches where Cheque clearing system is in vogue. Similarly, the rural branches should be totally exempt from the reporting requirements on TDS to avoid hardship to the small depositors. 

To sum up, Speaker, Sir, the entire budges canvass was very wide and inclusive. There are many bold and path-breaking initiatives which are long overdue. The underlying philosophy of growth with equity and human face has been well articulated in many initiatives relating to social and rural sectors. My suggestion to Finance Minister would be to bring about more improvements in data profile on allocations with exclusive reference to district-wise and constituency-wise so that many new Members of Parliament would be in a position to play a constructive role in translating the outlays of Budget into outcomes in their home constituencies. Before I conclude, I would like to draw my attention to Hon. Finance Minister again about my suggestion of ‘National Rural Credit Mission’ and ‘Urgent Revamping of Crop Insurance Scheme’.

I thank you, Speaker, Sir, for giving me and my party an opportunity to share our views and feedback on Budget 2005-06.

SHRI L. RAJAGOPAL : That is why, today, this UPA Government, through this Budget is talking about Bharat Nirman. Bharat Nirman does not mean that we are reconstructing India but we are trying to re-focus on what happened in the last six years, on the derailment and we are trying to bring back on the track and trying to re-focus on building India. That is why Bharat Nirman is the need of the day. It is not only the need of today but it was the need of the past and it will be the need of the future. That is the reason why all of us need to focus on Bharat Nirman and concentrate on the essential things for the common man like drinking water, water for irrigation, education for all, health to all and gainful employment to one and all. Our hon. Minister of Finance, Shri Chidambaram has said that ‘we need to take a leaf out of China’. Yes, it is not only a leaf, but I will tell you, we need to take a seed out of China and we have to plant it here so that seed can generate many such leaves which would transform India. The reason why I am telling you that we should take a leaf out of China is, it is not just to please our Left Parties but I am talking about the facts. 

In the last six years, if you look at the growth, you see what happened in the steel sector, cement sector, power sector and in exports and imports. I will give you some brief statistics. In the last six years, China has added more than 150 million tonnes of steel; we have added only seven million tonnes of steel – that too not because of new industries but because of enhancement of the old capacity. When it comes to cement, China has added 280 million tonnes and India has added only 23 million tonnes. When it comes to power, we had added 52 billion units of power whereas China has added 555 billion units of power. When it comes to exports, their exports are more than 593 billion dollars and our exports are only 64 billion dollars. If you take the imports, China’s imports are 561 billion dollars and our imports are 78 billion dollars. 

There is a need for tremendous growth and all-round development. That is why Madam Gandhi has said that we need to look at it not only with a human face but with a human heart. SHRI ASADUDDIN OWAISI (HYDERABAD): Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak. This is a full-fledged Budget presented by hon. Finance Minister after the UPA has come into power. In the last Lok Sabha elections held last year, people have voted decisively against the communal-led politics of BJP and for banks-led new economic policies. 

Sir, because of the shortage of time, I will restrict myself to seven points. The first point is regarding minority development. The Finance Minister has spoken in his speech that the equity of National Minority Development Finance Corporation will be increased, but if you look at the budgetary documents, especially page 41 of Expenditure Budget of 2005-06, you will find that for 2005-06, the budget allocation for NMDFC is only Rs. 19.60 crore. Last year it was Rs. 71 crore. The Finance Minister in his speech has said that the equity will be increased. But it has not been increased; it has been decreased. 

I would like to point out, through you, to the Government that in the year 2003-04, the budget given to Maulana Azad Education Foundation by the NDA Government was Rs. 13 crore. Last year, it was decreased to one crore of rupees and for this year, 2005-06, not a single paisa has been allocated.

The people are asking us about the allocations that have been made for the development of minorities. Sir, I would request the Government, through you, to increase the Budget of the National Minorities Development Finance Corporation (NMDFC). Its corpus fund should be increased to, at least, Rs. 1,000 crore. Maulana Azad Education Foundation (MAEF) was established exclusively for the educational development of the minorities. Its corpus fund should also be increased to Rs. 200 crore.

Thirdly, last year this Government had collected nearly Rs. 4,000 crore on account of a 2 per cent cess on education. At least, 2 per cent of Rs. 4,000 crore so collected should be given for the educational development of the minorities. The Finance Minister has stated that all the coaching centres will be given the work to teach the minorities to come forward for the competitive examinations. I welcome this step, but unless and until the Government comes forward and strengthens the Maulana Azad Education Foundation, and the National Minorities Development Finance Corporation (NMDFC), the education upliftment, and economic upliftment cannot take place. I was hearing the speech made by one hon. Member of the BJP, and he stated that it is minority appeasement, namely, allowing the minority students to go, and take coaching in specialised coaching centres. How can it be minority appeasement? The 2001 census is very clear that literacy level of muslims in India is 59.6 per cent. It is less than the national average. 

The work participation of muslims is the lowest in the whole country. So, I would request the hon. Finance Minister not to give us the fish, but to teach us how to catch the fish. This is the demand of the minorities, and smart words will not help us in this regard. 

This Government has got a mandate, and the mandate was against communal politics. The mandate was against all that had happened in the last six years. There was no development of the minorities during that period. I hope that the Finance Minister will respond to our request.

Fourthly, the hon. Finance Minister has talked about a growth of 67 per cent. In the last five years, after reading the Economic Survey, we have observed that there is only a jobless growth. The projection of a higher economic growth will not solve the unemployment problem, which is prevailing in our country. I would request that this jobless growth should end, and more focus should be given towards having an economic growth, which will provide equitable growth and employment opportunities.

Our party opposes FDI in mining. Joan Robinson, one of the renowned economists of the last century has stated that it is jeopardous to allow FDI in mining. It is because it is our natural resource, and they are exhaustible. I would request that the Government should utilise the intellectually skilled labour, and create a surplus. This surplus can be utilised to create the infrastructure.

Fifthly, our party opposes the pension fund. We cannot give pension fund to any foreign operator. It has two purposes. All sectors in the economy have their own macro-economic factors. The pension funds are still being utilised in the social sectors. We are also opposing the pension fund because the common man is politically empowered, and not legally empowered in it. I am saying this because in our legal system a common man has to spend lakhs of rupees to get justice. Hence, the claim of the Finance Minister that the pension fund will legally help them is untenable. I would also like to say that more stress should be given on higher education.

Lastly, he has stressed in his Budget speech about a famous tamil poem, and he has also recited it. I would say that wealth should be created for the minorities also. Please do not fall in the trap of these people and talk about minority appeasement. It is not a question of minority appeasement. We want justice to be done to us. 

Sir, I am concluding my speech. I have been sitting here for the last seven hours. under the provisions of Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India. Very unfortunately, the Government of India has not done anything tangible for the development of Bodoland Area and other tribal-dominated areas across the country over the past half a century period since Independence.

I would like to appeal to the Government of India that a good number of special packages for development should be announced for the Bodoland Territory in particular and for the tribal-dominated areas across the country in general. For the development and welfare of the tribal people of the whole country, a minimum of Rs. 1,00000 (one lakh crore) should be earmarked in the Central Budget, and a minimum of Rs. 10,000 crore should be earmarked for the development and welfare of the North-Eastern Region. For the development and welfare of the Bodoland Territory, a minimum of Rs. 1,000 crore should be earmarked and should be sanctioned by the Government of India to create necessary infrastructure. We do not have any roads; we do not have any hospitals; we do not have any drinking water facilities; and there is no electricity. You always talk about this project and that project at the national level, but your tall claims are meaningless for the Bodoland people. 

I, therefore, would like to request the Government of India to take appropriate steps to set up the following educational institutions of serious public importance :

A Bodoland Central University should be set up at Kokrajhar, which is the Headquarters of the Bodoland Territorial Areas District; (BTAD)

A Central Agricultural University at Kokrajhar;

A Medical College at Kokrajhar;

An Engineering College at Kokrajhar; and

An AIIMS-model Institute at Kokrajhar.

The Government of India has announced a policy to set up six AIIMS-model institutes. Why should they be set up only in six States, and why should such an Institute not be set up in Bodoland and in other tribal-dominated areas too? Why are you so miser? I strongly demand that some more AIIMS-model Institutes should be set up within tribal-dominated areas also, especially in the Bodoland area. 

The proposed Indian Institute of Management meant for the North-Eastern Region should be set up at Kokrajhar within the Bodoland Territory.

A National Institute of Information Technology also should be set up within the Bodoland area.

A National Institute of Textiles and Fashion Technology also should be set up within the Bodoland Territory because hundred per cent Bodoland girls and tribal women are born experts in weaving. Our Territory is very much rich in a special variety of silk known as ''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''Indi Silk - (Wild Silk).

A minimum of five numbers of polytechnic institutes should be set up within the BTAD;

A minimum of five numbers of ITIs should be set up within the BTAD;

A National Institute of Tourism and Hospitality Management also should be set up within the BTAD.

A Regional Institute of Bio-Technology should be set up at Kokrajhar;

Doordarshan Kendra at Kokrajhar should be upgraded into a full-fledged 

Doordarshan Kendra. There is a Low Power Transmitter Centre at Kokrajhar;

Why that Transmitter Centre should be of low power? Why cannot that be upgraded to a fulfledged transmitter just like the ones in Guwahati and Delhi? This is very unfortunate! 

Over the last more than 57 years since Independence, you could not do anything for the development and welfare of the tribal people. What kind of justice have you accorded to the tribal people in this country? This is the land of Mahatma Gandhi. You always claim that you all are Gandhians. What kind of allegiance do you owe to the Father of the Nation Mahatma Gandhi when you deny due justice to the tribal people of this great country whose forefathers had made a lot sacrifice during the freedom struggle. This is very unfortunate. 

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Please conclude. 

SHRI SANSUMA KHUNGGUR BWISWMUTHIARY : Sir, I would like to table the remaining portion of my speech. 

In the end, I would like to appeal to the Government of India to look at the endless tragedies and miseries being suffered and faced by several millions of the tribal people of this country. 

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Please sit down.

Through your honour, I would like the Union Finance Minister, in particular, and the present UPA Government at the Centre, as a whole, to take 

appropriate steps and prompt action to fulfil my long-pending genuine demands as mentioned hereunder :

A Special Central Assistance to the tune of minimum Rs.10,000 (Ten thousand) crore per annum should be allocated for the welfare and development of the Scheduled Tribes across the country.

A Special Central Assistance to the tune of minimum Rs. 1000 crore per annum should be allocated in favour of the ‘Bodoland Territorial Areas District’ – a constitutionally recognised backward tribal area created in 2003 in Assam under the provision of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution as a measure to help re-compensate the loss suffered by the concerned, neglected and deprived Bodo-Tribal Territory over the last half a century period since Independence considering the degree of the backwardness of the Bodoland Territory.

The Central Fund under the provision of Article 275(1) should be given directly to all the Autonomous District Councils created under the provision of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India with special mention to ‘Bodoland Territorial Areas District’ in Assam.

Out of the total Central Fund allocated for special economic development projects and programmes for North-Eastern Region under NLCPR, minimum of Rs. 500 crore per annum should be provided to the Bodoland Territorial Areas District considering the degree of the backwardness of the concerned Bodo-Tribal Area in question.

Out of the total Central Fund allocated for NEC, every year, minimum of Rs. 100 crore should be given to the ‘Bodoland Territorial Areas District’ in Assam to help create necessary infrastructure in the overall discriminated, deprived and neglected Bodoland Territory, although the same area is having Indo-Bhutan-international and Assam-West Bengal- interstate boundary attachment.

The NLCPR fund for N.E. Region should be enhanced up to Rs.10,000 crore per annum excluding the State Plan and other central/national projects/programmes.

The NEC fund also should be enhanced up to Rs.1000 crore per annum.

The Government of India should take appropriate action to declare ‘Bodoland Territory’ as a ‘Special Economic Zone’ (SEZ) in North-Eastern Region.

A few selective agro and forest based industries should be established within the ‘Bodoland Territory’.

Some food-processing industries also should be set up within the ‘Bodoland Terroritory’.

The Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station (BTPS), Salakati in Kokrajhar, a 240 Megawatt power generating project should be revived, renovated and re-run in the overall interest of the down-trodden Bodo-Tribal people of the Bodoland Territory.

The Centre should take appropriate steps for massive rural electrification in the Bodoland Territory, in particular, and also in all the Tribal dominated villages across the country, as a whole.

The Centre should take appropriate steps to construct, at least, 1000 kilometres of National Highways within the Bodoland Terriroty, and the East-West Route Corridor should be implemented through the original alignment as proposed by the NHAI, that is, through NH-31(c) and NH-31 along the Bengal Duars and the Bodoland-Assam Duars.

The Centre should take appropriate steps to help complete the half-done ‘Champamati and Dhanshri (Major river irrigation projects) under AIBP in BTAD by giving one-time adequate amount of Central Fund to the concerned languishing irrigation projects. Besides, the Union should take necessary action to create the necessary infrastructure on irrigation sector in BTAD area.

All villages should be connected with improved roads under the PMGSY in the BTAD area.

The Centre also should take necessary steps to provide telecom service facilities to all the people within the Bodoland Territory by creating the required infrastructure.

The Union Government of India should also take up some multi-purpose hydro-electric power and irrigation projects on some viable rivers originated in Bhutan and China and which flow through the Bodoland Territory.

The Union Government should take necessary steps to set up one domestic Airport at Kokrajhar and one International Airport within Bodoland Territory adjacent to Galegkhu in Bhutan Kingdom.

The Government of India should take appropriate action plans to address the perennial flood and river-erosion problems in the Bodoland Territory.

An Indo-China Trade Route/Road in Bhutan along our Bodoland Territory should be constructed. 

Necessity of setting up some specific educational institutions of serious public importance :

The following educational institutions should be set up by the Union Government of India in order to help boost the education sector within the Bodoland Territory also. 

A Bodoland Central University at Kokrajhar.

A Central Agriculture University at Kokrajhar.

A Medical College at Kokrajhar.

An engineering college at Kokrajhar.

An AIIMS Model Institute at Kokrajhar.

The Proposed IIM recently announced for NE Region should be set up at Kokrajhar.

A National Institute of Information Technology at Kokrajhar.

A National Institute of Textiles and Fashion Technology at Kokrajhar.

Minimum five numbers of polytechnic institutes within BTAD.

Minimum five numbers of ITIs within BTAD.

A National Institute of Tourism and Hospitality Management at Kokrajhar.

A Regional Institute of Bio-Technology at Kokrajhar.

The Doordarshan Kendra, Kokrajhar should be upgraded to a full-fledged Doordarshan Kendra.

AIR Station, Kokrajhar also should be upgraded to a full-fledged AIR Station.

A National Tribal Cultural Heritage Museum should be set up at Kokrajhar.

Tourism should be developed in BTAD.

Minimum of 100 hospitals with modern amenities and facilities should be set up within BTAD.

Special central assistance for the development of Bodo language and Bodo-medium education.

The Government of India should allocate minimum of Rs.500 crore per annum for the development of Bodo language and Bodo-medium education.

There should be a special package for the Tribal people across the country as mentioned here under:

A Central University for the Tribals should be set up in New Delhi.

A Central Medical University for Tribal people should be set up in New Delhi.

A National Institute of Information Technology for Tribal people in New Delhi.

A National Institute of Free-Examination Coaching of Tribal candidates in New Delhi.

As many as 10 nos. of Tribal Guest House Complexes in New Delhi.

As many as 10 nos. of Tribal hostels should be set up in New Delhi.

A National Level Tribal Development Authority should be set up under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister himself comprising all the ST MPs as Members.

Total allocation under Special Central Assistance for the welfare and development of the Tribal people across the country should be enhanced up to Rs.1,00,000 crore per annum.

A National Museum for Tribal Cultural Heritage should be set up in New Delhi.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Please conclude now.

*SHRI K.V. THANGKABALU (SALEM): Sir, the UPA Government came to power and the visionary leadership of Mrs. Sonia Gandhi under her dynamic leadership, the UPA parties and leaders jointly prepared a National Common Minimum Programme for the country as a governing instrument, which is one of the unique feature and will convert India as the tallest nation economically, socially & politically in the years to come.

Mr. Chidambaram has endeavoured a very thoughtful and meaningful Budget to implement the Common Minimum Programme and its aims and goals to the expected level and satisfaction. The Common Minimum Programme mandated the Government to maintain a growth rate of 7 per cent to 8 per cent a year, to promote investment, to create employment opportunities, accelerate fiscal consolidation and also greater emphasis on agriculture joined with manufacturing and infrastructure. The CMP also provides for greater access to education and healthcare. To support the weaker sections in the rural areas, the Finance Minister has promised one hundred days of employment to one person in each family is a milestone arrangement to help the poor. In the first year of UPA Government, in spite of a number of financial development activities taking place, the inflation rate went up to 8.7 per cent in the month of August, 2004. But, due to the best management efforts and effective control mechanism, Mr. Chidambaram was able to bring down the inflation rate to a level of 5.0 per cent, which is one per cent lower than what it was in the same week of previous year. He restored the confidence among investors in the year 2004-05. Today, the non-food credit has gone up by 22.2 per cent. 

In the last year’s Budget, both the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister, earmarked agricultural credit to the tune of Rs. 1,05,000 crore. This was one of 

*Speech was aid on the Table.

the greatest helps to the agrarian community, who is longing for better facilities and loans availability. 

Education loans were given to the students by the Finance Minister. I personally thank him for having agreed to my suggestions that the students from poor community all over the country should get education loans. The Finance Minister’s announcement, as also the implementation, of this noble cause of giving loans to thousands and millions of needy young boys and girls throughout the country is a welcome step. This will go a long way in promoting higher standard of educational facilities, particularly to the weaker sections of our society. The families and the students are blessing our Hon. Finance Minister for this humane approach.

I also thank and appreciate that the plan allocations for the economic year 2005-06 at Rs. 18337 crore for education, Rs. 19334 crore for rural development, fertilizer subsidies to the tune of Rs. 6254 crore and health sector has got Rs. 10280 crore. These are the main component of our community which has got a fair deal from the Finance Minister.

The National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme has got a boost by providing Rs. 5400 crore as a cash component and Rs. 50 lakh metric tonnes of foodgrains worth another Rs. 5600 crore. Thus a total sum of Rs. 1100 crore for this scheme is one of the very important areas where crore of unemployed people will get security and employment in an honourable livelihood. 

The Mid-day Meal Scheme was introduced in the State of Tamil Nadu by the late lamented leader Karma Veerar Kamraj, the then Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, and today the Government of India provide Rs. 3010 crore for the Mid-Day Meal Scheme to enhance the health of eleven crore young children. I request the hon. Finance Minister to make it compulsory for all the schools all over the country and allocate more funds for this noble scheme. Thereby, we can create confidence and health creation to our children.

The Congress Government, led by Shri Narasimha Rao during 1991-96 period, initiated Rajiv Gandhi Drinking Water Mission. For this programme, the Finance Minister has provided an outlay of Rs. 4750 crore for 2005-06 to cover the uncovered 31355 rural habitations. I also urge the Finance Minister to announce a time-bound programme, i.e., within five years, by 2009, all habitations – rural and urban – in our country must get potable drinking water by all means. 

The NCMP has clearly demarcated that our Government will provide the necessary funds to promote the SC, ST, OBC and minority communities in all totality, i.e., socially, economically and educationally forward movement for this weaker section. I am thankful to the Finance Minister that this year he has done his best by providing Rs. 6253 crore for only Sc and ST development schemes and programmes. This is very much welcome and I urge him to earmark more funds for SC/ST communities.

But, to my surprise, the Finance Minister has forgotten the promise made to the OBCs by the NCMP, i.e., there is no allocation whatsoever to this 60 per cent population of our country, which is not only the weakest among the weaker sections in all terms – i.e., socially, educationally and economically.

There is no separate Ministry for the OBCs. There is no Standing Committee in Parliament to care to cater to the needs of these millions of backward-class people in our country. I urge upon the Finance, at least in its reply to the Budget debate, to announce a substantial allocation to the backward class community for their development in this year itself. 

The minorities of our society are always getting due consideration and encouragement by all means for the betterment by our UPA Government, for which I am thankful to the UPA leadership.

His Excellency, the President of India, in his Address to the Parliament outlined a vision for Bharat Nirman under the dynamic leadership of UPA Government. Our goals are to bring additional one crore hectares under assured irrigation, to connect all the villages that have a population of one thousand and in hilly and tribal areas five hundred with roads. Sixty lakhs additional houses for the poor drinking water to the remaining 74,000 habitations. 1,25,000 villages to get electricity and also 2.3 crore household electricity connection. 66,800 villages are to be connected by telephones. These are the main objects of Bharat Nirman Programme. This will be completed by the year 2009. This is one of the very important milestone achievements. If we do this, and I hope that our Government will be able to achieve, it will bring laurels to the community. 

The farm insurance programme is one of the important components of the Budget. I appeal the Finance Minister that an individual farmer, who is affected by plague, natural calamity or drought, be given full advantage of insurance cover so that affected agricultural people are able to refurbish their livelihood in an honourable way. Micro Finance Programme through self-help groups is also laudable. Finance Minister’s proposal to enhance the target for credit linking in 2005-06 to the tune of 2.5 lakh shgs. is the commitment from the bottom of his heart. I welcome this initiative. Both women and men must join in this endeavour to promote for betterment.

Employment generation through various means is very much needed to solve unemployment problem in this country. One area where we can create more employment schemes next to agriculture textiles. In the agrarian sector - we can create agri-business programmes through agro-based industries, such as food processing etc. Also the Government’s programme of investing to the tune of Rs. 33,000 crore is a welcome feature in textile industry.

The other employment protection is the Khadi and village industry, which has the maximum possible avenues in creating new jobs to the rural community. Our Government is alive of this situation and my request to the Finance Minister is to increase the Budget allocation for this sector especially.

The other area of concern is SSI sector. Today, majority of SSI units are closed in the country due to want of funds. Upgradation could not be completed and they could not compete with the international competition. The liberalisation has brought many good things to the country and, at the same time, there is the other side effect of losing our traditionally small industrial ventures to lose its place. Hence, I appeal to the Finance Minister that special care is taken to help the SSI sector by infusing the necessary funds, also the technological back-up, so that hundreds of new units and employment generation is created in the rural areas. The minimum limit of one crore to three crore and subsidy from 15 per cent to 25 per cent is a must. I hope you will help this sector.

Now, I come to the banking sector. Sir, in your Budget, you have mentioned that the top-most bank of our country, i.e., the State Bank of India, ranks 82nd in terms of business in the international arena. The banking sector is to be re-oriented to meet the challenges and needs of the common man. That is a humane face is the need of the hour. Our beloved leader, Mrs. Indira Gandhi, nationalised the banks to suit the needs of the common man, particularly the rural people. In spite of our best efforts, the banking people, at all levels, ae still thinking that they are the masters and they do not think that they are serving the people. The attitude is negative and arrogant by all means. You have ordered that the agricultural community should get loans without any difficult also the students. But, in real terms, we find the officers of the banking system are not implementing the way you want and the way the UPA leadership wants to help the poor people. I urge you to direct all the bankers – the public sector, rural banks and co-operatives – to meet the requirements as per the norms.

The banking system has to implement the rules prescribed by the RBI and the Government of India. But, they are not doing so and also there are a lot of complaints of mismanagement, misbehaviour and supporting only the rich. I personally can report you a number of instances where genuine people are not getting their due through the system. Your indulgence and order to set right the sector is very much urgent.

The centrally sponsored schemes are to be monitored by the respective MPs. The state Governments are misusing the funds, which are meant for this programme by selecting their own ways and means the beneficiaries. This should be stopped forthwith and the Members of Parliament should be empowered to select, administer and monitor the programmes by this way only the centrally sponsored schemes will have their total implementation.

You have increased the PF share from 8.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent thereby our commitment to the working class is honoured.

Sir, in my constituency, Selam Steel Plant, a public sector undertaking is there and it needs your blessing, your support by ordering all your department needs of coin making so that the coin blanking machine in Selam Steel Plant will have the benefit of full utility.

The Watershed Programme is one of the important areas and you are very considerate about developing water body in the country. I request your goodself to announce more amount for implementing the water bodies and develop new water management programme so that we can save, use and conserve water for the community. 

The linking of rivers is one of the most urgent and important programme, which will help not only stopping the wastage but also improving our agriculture, drinking water utility and enhancing the food production for our own needs and also the exports. This gigantic programme needs your support and initiatives and I hope you will do good to this area also.

I personally congratulate to you for the bold steps you have taken to implement the CMP and enhance the prestige of the leadership of Smt. Sonia Gandhi and Dr. Manmohan Singh.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Shri Athawale, first of all you should go to your seat. If you have any difficulty in speaking from there, I can allow you to speak from here. If there is no difficulty, please go to your seat.

Finance Minister for this excellent Budget, which takes care of the needs of all sections of society. This pro-poor Budget is targeted to remove poverty and deals with one of the biggest problems of our country, that is, unemployment.

The National Rural Guarantee Scheme would prove a boon to the unskilled rural people. The new jobs are to be created by enhancing the irrigation facilities in agricultural sector. Investment in food processing industries, textile industries, IT sector and construction sector would create lakhs of new jobs in the years to come.

It is high time that we should devote our attention to rural healthcare. The launching of National Rural Health Mission is a welcome step. The poor health infrastructure in rural areas is a cause of concern. The sub-centres are unmanned. The public health centres does not have sufficient number of doctors and nurses. The community health centres do not have gynaecologists, paediatricians and anaesthetists. These health centres lack in equipment, that is, ex-ray machines, blood analysers and other investigating facilities. The budget for medicine has to be increased. Immunization and nutrition programme needs to be strengthened. We have to think a lot more about the population control programme. The time has come when young couple in rural India is trying to adopt contraceptives and other family planning methods. There is a great-unmet need. Our healthcare delivery system has to be strengthened so that the maternal and infant mortality could be reduced. The general public, by and large, has appreciated the proposal of imposing cess on tobacco, cigarettes and gutkas. We must increase public awareness about the damage being caused by using these tobacco products. We have to put a ban on the advertisement of these items on TV and other media.

*Speech was laid on the Table.

Enhancement the scope of Antyodaya Anna Yojana, Integrated Child Development Scheme, and Mid-Day Meal Programme are all targeted keeping in mind the upliftment of the poor brethren and sisters. In the next four years, the face of villages must change. The dream of Bharat Nirman must become a reality. This new deal to change the face of Rural India should not remain a slogan, but it should be reflected in action.

Today, the face of villages has become dirtier day by day. The village streets are full of mud. It does not mean that there is no drainage system. A large number of villages are not even remotely connected with roads. The telephone connectivity becomes a daydream in the desert and hilly areas of Rajasthan.

The previous National Democratic Alliance Government did not do anything for the rural areas. The targets envisaged in the Bharat Nirman have to be achieved by the UPA Government.

Sir, I would like to draw your kind attention to my home State of Rajasthan. By all standards and parameters, Rajasthan is the most backward State in the country. Rajasthan is one of the largest States in the country. Most parts of Rajasthan are drought-prone areas. The drought situation becomes a synonymous for the Western Rajasthan. Nothing has been done to combat and check this menace of drought. A large number of people migrate from Western Rajasthan to Gujarat and other areas in search of jobs. It is a cattle-breeding area. It has also the grazing land and forestation. Rajasthan canal, which is our lifeline, needs to be completed as soon as possible. For this, adequate Budget allotments have to be made.

There is a large reserve of oil in the western part of Rajasthan. Barmer and Sanchore Basin have large reserves of oil, and they could probably change the future of poor Rajasthan. HPCL has proposed to set up an oil refinery in Rajasthan. Almost all the people of Rajasthan are disappointed by the attitude adopted by the hon. Petroleum Minister, because Rajasthan does not find any priority in his frame of mind.

Sir, I would like to request, through you, Sir, to consider installing an oil refinery in Rajasthan at the earliest. This project would open up new job opportunities for thousands of people of Rajasthan.

I would urge upon the hon. Finance Minister to consider giving special financial package to Rajasthan. I would like to request to make amendments in the Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula, on whose basis, the transfer of grants from Centre to States is done. In this existing formula, due weightage needs to be given to areas, as the cost of delivery of service is more due to large area and low density of population.

Sixty per cent Rajasthan is desert. Special weightage should be given to hilly areas. A large population of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes residing in Rajasthan also needs special consideration.

In the end, I would like to draw the kind attention of the hon. Finance Minister to my constituency Alwar. Though this year we were hoping for a good harvest of mustard and wheat, but the last week’s hailstorm damaged the whole crop. I would like to request that a special team should be sent to this area and drought should be declared. Compensation should also be given to farmers. The relief works should also be started as early as possible.

The industrial town Bhiwari needs special attention. The Malviya Industrial Area in Alwar was the vibrant and dynamic industrial area once upon a time. This area is lying dormant and quiet. Most of the factories in this area are closed. The whole area is deserted. The workers and labourers have become jobless in the past few years.

I would like to request the hon. Finance Minister to constitute a special team or a task force to examine the causes of closure of industries in Malviya Industrial Area of Alwar. This team should suggest ways as to how the industries can be revived and restarted. We should also provide special incentives and tax benefits to industries in this area.

Although Alwar is a part of the National Capital Region Territory but so far it has not received any special financial assistance or any package from the hon. Urban Development Minister. We are paying higher prices of petrol and diesel, but we are not getting any benefit in the development of infrastructure, roads, industries, educational institutions and other civil amenities. It has the vast potential for starting the agro-based industries. I sincerely hope that the Central Government would do all possible efforts in this direction.

SHRI K. FRANCIS GEORGE (IDUKKI): Sir, I rise to support the Budget presented by the hon. Finance Minister for the year 2005-06. At the very outset, I would like to congratulate the Minister for touching every aspect of the National Common Minimum Programme in his Budget speech. He had spent most of the time and space in his Budget speech towards the agriculture sector. Very rightly so because agriculture is the backbone of our economy. 

Nevertheless, I am constrained to point out certain glaring omissions in the Budget speech as far as the agriculture sector of our economy is concerned. Out of the total outlay of Rs. 5,14,344 crore, the allotment for agriculture sector is only Rs. 6,949 crore, which translates to 1.25 per cent of the total outlay. SHRI K. FRANCIS GEORGE : Sir, there has been a mention about National Rural Employment Programme. This Programme has to be linked with skill development. There is a mention about the skill development in the Budget speech. It has to be linked with this particular Programme.

The Finance Minister has very generously mentioned about the plantation sector. The plantation sector is also facing a severe crisis for the last three or four years. Over a lakh of plantation workers are out of job throughout the country. In my constituency, Idukki district of Kerala, eighteen plantations have been closed. More than thirty thousand workers are jobless for the past three years. More rejuvenation and re-plantation is not going to solve the problem. The hon. Finance Minister should look at the human problem. Rejuvenating and replanting tea bushes or coffee plants by itself is not going to solve the problem of the plantation sector.

We have to open the plantations. We have to give work to the plantation labours. The State itself cannot do that. There has to be liberal Central assistance. I hope the hon. Finance Minister will take a liberal approach to this very vexing problem.

There has been mention about creating a knowledge centre and the National Fund for Strategic Agricultural Research. These are very welcome steps. When we think of the knowledge centre in every village, we have to think of one thing. The Dr. Swaminathan Committee mentioned about establishing virtual universities, linking all the villages through satellites, using the Doordarshan and the local channels to disseminate knowledge in the agricultural sector for the benefit of the rural farmers.

There has been mention about the PURA – Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas – Scheme. This is a very ambitious programme which has been mentioned in the President’s Speech. This is the one programme which is always being talked about by the hon. Rashtrapathi ji. Providing Urban Amenities in rural Areas is his pet programme. The hon. Finance Minister says in his speech that there is going to be only a few pilot projects. Elaborate exercises have been carried out throughout the country connected with panchayats bordering municipalities. I would request the hon. Finance Minister to sanction all these projects that have been brought to the Central Rural Development Ministry in connection with the PURA Scheme.… (Interruption)

*SHRI LALIT MOHAN SUKLABAIDYA (KARIMGANJ): Sir, I defend the Union Budget for 2005-06 for its pragmatic and farsighted approach concerning the immediate needs and the future growth of our country. The Budget is a balanced one focusing its attention on the growth and social justice.

The transition of our country from a Developing State to a Developed State, as envisaged by 2010, is only possibly by converting our huge human resource into human capital. Keeping this in mind, the hon. Finance Minister has doubled the allocation for the education sector. 

Last year, the allocation for the education sector was of the order of Rs. 8,225 crore. This year, the hon. Finance Minister has increased it to Rs. 18,337 crore. His thrust in education is further envisaged, in his proposal, for enhancement of scholarship for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in selected institutions, and also in introdution of Rajiv Gandhi Fellowship Scheme for the Scheduled Caste students, who are doing M. Phil and Ph.D. The hon. Finance Minister has also allotted funds for upgrading Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore into a world-class University.

About 100 Industrial Training Institutions (ITIs) will be upgraded, out of which 67 will be linked with industries. All these attempts are aiming at the conversion of human resource into human capital.

The hon. Finance Minister has extended his helping hand to all segments of our society. The salaried class and senior citizens are happy for getting income tax relief. The business class is also happy for getting tax relief in certain sectors and various incentives for growth orientation.

The unique feature of the Budget is that, for the first time, it takes into consideration the gender equality. The hon. Finance Minister is trying to reduce the long-existing discrimination of status between men and women.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

Eighty per cent of our population is rural. The hon. Finance Minister has made some provisions, which were long awaited, for their upliftment and development. For diversification of agriculture, a National Fund of Rs. 50 crore is earmarked to implement the recommendation of Task Force. Before 15 August, 2007, every village will be covered with a Knowledge Centre with the help of NABARD.

An amount of Rs. 11,000 crore have been allotted for the employment generation. One-Hundred-Fifty districts are to be covered under the Food for Work Programme, 60 lakh new houses are going to be constructed, 74,000 villages will be supplied with potable drinking water, 125,000 villages are going to be electrified and 16,822 villages will get the telephone facilities. As per the existing population norms, more than 1.88 Anganwadi Centres are going to be set up, is a welcome step.

All villages, which are having a population of more than 1000 people, are to come within the roadmap of India. In the case of tribal areas, the population criterion is 500. Moreover, one crore hectare of land will come under the guaranteed irrigation system. There will be unprecedented investment in providing these benefits in rural area which is no doubt a bold step to convert the rural area into a growth engine. The economy will be dynamic only when the purchasing power of the rural population is increased. These steps will reduce unemployment directly and indirectly, and generate income in the rural sector.

Sir, we are in Assam suffering from the problem of financing education. Thousands of schools and colleges, where teachers are rendering honorary service for a long time, could not be taken over due to shortage of funds. There is unrest among the teachers’ community as a whole. I would like to request the hon. Finance Minister to make special provision so that our State government can take over some schools and colleges, which were recognised long back but could not be taken over due to paucity of funds.

Since there is provision for drinking water, rural electrification, housing and connectivity of villages, we see a ray of hope for our people staying in rural areas. I would like to request the hon. Finance Minister to look into the problems, which we are facing in the bordering districts and allot adequate funds so that the basic problems of the rural people could be alleviated.

We have our heritage in agriculture and tea industry. We want these two sectors should be developed at par with other parts of the country. The imbalance of development should be reduced.

We are joyful that provisions are made in the Budget for Barak and Brahmaputra Rivers for protecting us from the devastating floods. We are also happy for declaring the long pending Lumbding-Badarpur Railway section along with Silchar-Tupul and Kumarghat-Agartala as national projects, and also for the specific provisions made for national highway developments in the North-Eastern States. We will be more happy on completion of the projects.

Revival of waterways for carrying goods for Kolkata is a long-standing demand of the people of South Assam. This will also help Tripura and Manipur. I urge upon the hon. Prime Minister to consider our demand for reviving waterways from Barak-Kushiaqra to the Hoogly River in Kolkata through Bangladesh.

Sir, my constituency covers two revenue Districts – Karimganj, Hailakandi, and part of Cachar District, which is a very backward area in the State. More than half of the boundary of my constituency is with Bangladesh. I hope that the districts of my constituency are included in the list of backward districts for which special provision of Rs. 500 crore are made. If it is not included, then I would like to request you to kindly include all the three districts, that is, Karimganj, Hailakandi and Cachar for special grants under the provision for backward region.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Now, I would request Shrimati K. Rani to speak for only two minutes.

SHRIMATI K. RANI (RASIPURAM): Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to put forth my views on the General Budget for the year 2005-06.

Like the Budget of the last year, this Budget has also, to a great extent, proved to be a popular Budget brought by our prudent Finance Minister under the overall guidance of our charismatic leader Madam Sonia Gandhi, the Chairperson of the UPA, and under the leadership of the Prime Minister Dr. manmohan Singh.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: You are reading your speech. You can lay it on the Table of the House.

SHRIMATI K. RANI : In this Budget, there has been a special focus on the social, economic and educational betterment of the minorities and the SC/ST communities. Numerous provisions have been made to provide better education to minorities such as the percentage of Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya will be opened in predominantly minority districts or development blocks. 

These are the most commendable aspects of this Budget. Besides this, a significant increase of Rs.1335 crore has been made in the Budget allocation as compared to that in the last year for the Mid-Day Meal Scheme for school children.

The reputed private coaching institutions have been allowed to participate in various pre-examination coaching schemes already being run by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and the Ministry of Human Resources Development for the minority students. Similarly, in it, a new scheme has been formulated to provide better higher educational opportunities to the SC and ST students. A list of some reputed educational/vocational institutions will be prepared for this purpose in which much more increased scholarship will be given to the SC/ST students to pay the fee, meet the day to day educational expenditure and to purchase books and computer. This Budget provides for the launching of Rajiv Gandhi Fellowship for SC/ST students doing Ph.D or M.Phil in some selected Universities. In Tamil Nadu, there are a large number of SC/ST students who are studying in professional colleges. They are not in a position to pay the fees on their own. So, they are approaching the nationalised banks to get loans. But the bank authorities are demanding security for the same. Even if they provide the necessary security, the bank officers are not treating them honourably and only 10 per cent of the students are getting loans. So, I would request the hon. Finance Minister to issue suitable instructions to all the bank authorities to sanction loans to SC/ST students pursuing higher education. If it is done, all the SC/ST students and their families would be highly grateful to the hon. Finance Minister.

It appears from the Budget that despite continuing its agenda of economic reforms, the Government has tried its level best to please the people of all the sections of the society.

In this Budget, the Finance Minister has shown greater concern for social sector by announcing a National Rural Health Mission, which aims at strengthening of primary health services based on the community ownership. Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme is also being launched to generate jobs in villages.

In this Budget, substantial tax relief has been given to the salaried class people. On a salary of Rs.1.5 lakh, for instance, there is a saving of Rs.8,000 as income tax has been brought down from Rs.13,000 to Rs.5,000. For those who are self-employed, income tax saving is greater as the tax is down from Rs.19,000 to Rs.5,000. In this Budget, the Finance Minister has sought to materialise the promises made to the common man in the UPA’s Common Minimum Programme.

The main thrust of this Budget is on promoting investment, generating employment, accelerating fiscal consolidation and strengthening the infrastructure in rural as well as urban areas. It is a budget full of positives, and I hope it would be instrumental in higher economic growth, thereby increasing employment during the year 2005-06. 

With these words, I support this Budget. 

*SHRI RAYAPATI SAMBASIVA RAO (GUNTUR): Hon. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, first of all, I would like to congratulate the hon. Finance Minister, who under the able guidance of hon. Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh and Chairperson of UPA, Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, has presented a people-friendly Budget for the year 2005-06.

Sir, I welcome the Budget and I heartily congratulate the hon. Finance Minister for rural-development-oriented proposal by him.

At the outset, the Budget is devoid of concrete measures to help reasonable and remunerative prices for farm produce. It lacks effective market regulation to ensure payment of those prices in order to check exploitation of the producers by the monopoly traders or industry and vested interests.

Hon. Finance Minister proposed to introduce a new scheme called "Development and Strengthening of Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure" and has not specified the supportive services offered.

Often learned economists and scientists talk about higher yields, productivity and quality etc. But, unfortunately they do not talk about the prices to be paid to farm produce. Producers should be enabled to secure fair prices. Farm workers should get fair wages, handloom weavers should get fair prices for their produce and rural artisans should get fair prices for their products. Unless these are ensured, the purchasing capacity of the rural people cannot be improved. It is highly improper to expect rural people to live on doles and subsidies. The money is to be pumped into the pockets of all kinds of producers in the rural sector. Only then their purchasing capacity will improve to procure the requirement of their choice, their self-respect and dignity would be preserved and their individuality in the society would be maintained. 

Poverty alleviation is possible only with self-employment, self-earnings and self-purchasings to meet the needs of their families. The rural people should 

* Speech was laid on the Table.

not be left to beg for credit from individuals or institutions. Rural people should be enabled to live and transact their operations with their own self-finance and to carry own their production activities with their own self-finance on the strength of their production, but not at the mercy of the private sector. The policy and programme of the State should aim to achieve the independent and self-respecting rural sector. 

Even after 60 years of swaraj, we failed in all respects to adopt a realistic, complete, comprehensive and progressive policy for the improvement of the lot of the rural masses. It is indeed a pity. The flag of India should fly high in the high skies of globe taking advantage of enormous natural resources, healthy climatic conditions and toiling masses who believe in hard work, dharma and satyam with rich culture for the last 5,000 years.

The consistent agitation for parity prices for rural masses has become a cry of the father’s of rural champions in India and is in the wilderness. I would like to appeal to the hon. Finance Minister to consider steps to be taken to avoid exploitation of the rural sector by the organised and harsh traders. There must be a parity between the prices paid to the rural producers and retail prices to be paid by the consumers for the end products to minimise the exploitation and to ensure fair justice to the rural masses.

I would like to appeal to the hon. Finance Minister to consider the immediate need to take steps to bring about a comprehensive and radical reformation for regulating marketing of all the farm produce of commercial foodgrains etc. Government of India should keep Rs.100 crore of each for chillies and for tobacco crop to intervene in the market, whenever market falls drastically. This will help the farmers from the distress sales.

I would like to request the hon. Finance Minister to come forward to mitigate the sufferings of the rural people.
