*DR. C. KRISHNAN (POLLACHI): Sir, at the very out set, I congratulate our Finance Minister on behalf of MDMK party headed Thiru Vaiko for presenting a pro-poor people budget.

Sethu Samuthiram Canal Project

The most needed mega project is Sethu Samuthiram Canal Project for Tamilnadu which is being kept idle by some vested interests who are working against the implementation of the big project which will evolve much of job opportunities of Tamilian as well as improvement in business circle. The Government of Tamilnadu is yet to give a green signal to this volumeness project. Herein I wish to bring in historical background of the project. Late Thiru. Arignar Annadurai Former Chief Minister of Tamilnadu was very much interested in this project which was thought of by the English people about 130 years ago. Thiru Vaiko my leader on the stage of a rally in Madras organised on the occasion of Birthday of Thiru. C.N. Annadurai where former Prime Minister Thiru. A.B. Vajpayee was also present on 15th September 1998 on the personal request of my leader Thiru Vaiko as a true follower of the footsteps of great Anna. Former Prime Minister Thiru. A.B. Vajpayee announced that the project will be taken up and implemented.

Inter-linking of Rivers

To make a small note on expenditure on irrigation and flood control 355 crores real expenditure and 88.2 crores is envisaged.

My comment is that; on one side water is needed for irrigation purposes, No doubt, further a good amount is spared for flood situation in the country. Why not we plan the flood-ridden rivers to be diverted to the drought prone and dry areas of the country by digging long canals with a fore sight for the future agricultural development in the country.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

To create a consensus of opinion and awareness about the Inter-linking of rivers my leader thiru. Vaiko made a prestigious walk in our own state of Tamilnadu from Tirunelveli to Chennai 1200 kms and conducted Farmers and Farm Labourers Conference meetings at Palladam (Coimbatore). Vedasandur (Dindugal) and also made a purposeful visit to Kerala with a view of improving Water Resources for both the states.

This may be called also as Inter-linking of rivers from flood-ridden rivers into drought prone area as said above.

But I am disappointed that there is no mention about the linking of rivers in the budget.

Agriculture

Since our country is dependent on agriculture, the agriculturists have to be helped by extending minimum loans by adopting simplified procedures without insisting for collateral security at a comparatively cheaper rate of interest without any hurdles. The prospects of agriculture is purely dependent on the monsoon and if the monsoon fails, the agricultural activities comes to a standstill resulting in no revenue is earned, and under circumstances the agriculturists finding it very hard even to meet their daily livelihood. Since no revenue is earned, the agriculturists may not be in a position to repay the loans. Penal interest is a burden for the farmers. My appeal to the government is that the whole principal amount and the interest thereon should be waived in the drought-hit areas.

Social Measures

This budget welcomed by the rural folk because of the following Rural Infrastructure Project proposed:

Rural Housing (Indira Awas Yojana) wherein Rs. 250 crores increase in expenditure announced.

Universal Service Obligation with the objective of providing telephone facilities in rural areas Rs. 1200 crores.

Additional budgetary support to the tune of Rs. 1600 crore under PMGSY.

The expenditure on National Highways Development Projects Rs. 6,221.04 crores.

Rural electrification will cover 1.25 lakhs villages in five years Rs. 1100 provided, even though allocation of fund is awaited.

Agricultural Sector needs second thought about food security for the country as there is diversification of agricultural production to non-foodgrains especially horticultural production may be remunerative but there is fear about food security and production of foodgrains in a safe atmosphere.

Education is budgeted at Rs. 7538 crores it is worthwhile when we consider the status of our country’s literacy average, comparing to developed countries. We stand at 106 stage. Each village shall have a computer-oriented multipurpose community centre to create awareness among the public.

The proposal to increase excise duty rate on cigarettes by about 10% and the imposition of surcharge on other tobacco products.

Gender budgetary allocation of women and children for

Elementary education for girl child

Improving the working conditions of women labour

Social Justice and Women Empowerment 

Allocation of fund in the Ministry of Social Justice and Women Empowerment, also SGSY and SGRY.

Safety Matches 

Eight thousands Hand made matches industry units are there which are providing employment to 10 lakhs labours directly in four drought prone districts in Tamil Nadu. By reducing tax from 16% to 12% for the machine made matches 

the hand made match industry is struggling due to heavy competition from the machine made match industry. I request the Hand made match may be saved by allocating subsidise materials to Cooperative societies.

Tax on cash withdrawal

In this budget our Hon’ble Finance Minister proposed to levy a 0.01% tax on every withdrawal of Rs. 10,000 and above from the bank, it may be considered to raise the minimum level to Rs. 1,00,000/- and above.

*SHRI G. KARUNAKARA REDDY (BELLARY): Sir, I am opposing this Budget because it has brought very much unhappiness and no word has been put in this Budget about inter-linking of rivers project. The crores of farmers are looking towards this Budget because it not only solves the irrigation problems but also the water problems of the crores of people of this country. The Congress Party has ruled the country for nearly 46 years and they have not implemented this inter-linking of Rivers Project. It is an important matter nationally and this Project should be speeded up. In some areas, there is flood and in some other areas, there is drought. This uneven situation causes great problems to the people and this Project should be taken up very seriously and immediately on a war-footing basis. Sir, everybody says that the farmers are the backbone of the country but we are not giving importance to this Project of inter-linking of rivers. Many say that Green Revolution has been brought. I think, only with the inter-linking of the rivers project, Green Revolution will be brought.

I come to the most important point, that is the crop loan of the farmers. The crop loan, which is required by the farmers, exactly is not given by the banks. Only partial amount is given to the farmers. For example, Chilly irrigated the actual cost of cultivation per hectare is Rs. 40,000/- but the farmers get only Rs. 30,000/-, which means that the farmers cannot meet their crop requirements fully. For the rest of the amount, the farmers have to go for private money-lenders and the private money lenders charge interest of nearly 36 per cent, which the poor farmers facing great difficulties to repay the loan and the interest amount. So, I would request the hon. Finance Minister to give direction to the banks asking them to give full amount which is required by the farmers as the farmers are getting a part of it. Many States are affected due to drought during the last four years and the farmers are facing great difficulties in getting the return for their produce.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

Then, I would come to the point that the interest rate and other charges being paid by the farmers for this crop loan. The farmers have to pay 20.2 per cent towards insurance premium for chilly-dry, 17.20 per cent towards insurance premium for chilly-irrigated; 11 per cent towards insurance premium for onion, 13.50 per cent towards insurance premium for cotton-dry and 9.65 per cent towards insurance premium for cotton-irrigated, which is very much higher in percentage. Like this, they have to pay 10.25 per cent as interest cost for all products. I appreciate that the Minister has brought down the excise duty to nil to IT sector to encourage the IT industry, which is in the higher side. I urge upon the Finance Minister to apply the same formula for the poor farmers also by way of reducing the insurance premium at the rate of 2 per cent and the rate of interest to 5 per cent on all crop loans, so that the small farmers will be benefited greatly. I would also suggest that the cost of stamp duty for mortgage and other charges, which is now being charged at 2 per cent, should be removed at all.

Sir, Bellary District, which is also a backward district in Karnataka, is one of the worst-drought affected Districts in the State, especially for the last five years. The people are facing a lot of difficulties for their livelihood. I urge upon the Minister to include Bellary District under the National Food for Work Programme so that the people can earn little money for running their life.

Since Bellary District is also a backward district, it has to be included in the Rashtriya Samvikas Yojana for the Development of the District.

The Union Government is allocating Rs. 3645 for supplementing the States in their efforts to provide safe-drinking water to all rural habitations. I would like to mention that in Bellary, nearly 90 per cent fluoride contaminated water is being supplied, which causes great health problems to the people. I would suggest that a huge amount be allotted to Bellary District, Karnataka, for providing safe-drinking water to the people.

Sir, I am given to understand that under the Rural Sanitation Programme, an amount of Rs. 625/- is being given per house for the people living below poverty line in Bellary District. It is very difficult to provide rural sanitation with this small amount. I urge upon the Minister that this amount should be increased to Rs. 4,000/- per house for the people living below the poverty line.

Sir, the Finance Minister has allocated a sum of Rs. 3010 crore for Mid-Day meal Programme, which I feel is very much low. In Bellary District, Karnataka, a sum of Re. 1 is being given per student for this Mid-Day Meal Scheme. The students are not able to get proper healthy food because of this low amount. I suggest that this amount should be increased to Rs. 5 per student so that the students, who are the future younger generation, can get healthy food. 

Sir, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, which is meant for development of education in the country, especially in rural areas, is a welcome step. I visited personally nearly 90 per cent of the schools in my Bellary Constituency. The classrooms in these schools are in a bad condition, and these classrooms should be repaired immediately. Many school students in Bellary Constituency, Karnataka are facing lot of difficulties due to non-availability of proper classrooms. The students of the class are increased to a great extent. Nearly 100 students are studying in a single class but no classrooms are available for occupying these students. Sir, the Central Government have not taken any step to provide proper classrooms to these students and the fund available for this purpose is very much shortage. There is an urgent need to construct at least 3 classrooms in each school. I urge upon the Minister to provide sufficient funds for construction of classrooms immediately. 

In the month of October-November and March-April, there is a big water crisis in Karnataka, especially in Bellary District. The farmers are not getting proper water supply for their crops. The farmers are frequently agitating for not providing water to them. The storage capacity of the Tungabhadra Dam is drastically reduced nearly by 30 TMC because of silt formation in the Dam. There is an urgent need to construct 7 mini Dams of capacity of 13 TMC for which the Government of Karnataka has made survey and made estimates. An amount of Rs.650 crore is needed for this purpose. I urge upon the Union Government to provide necessary financial assistance to the State Government of Karnataka for clearing this silt and to increase the storage capacity of the Tungabhadra Dam for the benefit of farmers.

The farmers in Karnataka, especially in Bellary, are facing great difficulties to lead their life as they are not able to produce crops due to drought for last more than five years and in the absence of the canal system. In some drought affected/ dry areas, farmers are getting small quantity of iron ore in agricultural land within 3 to 5 feet and they are doing it manually. But procedure for getting permission for this mining is very lengthy that they should get permission from the State Government and then from the Central Government. There is an urgent need to simplify of procedure so that farmers can earn little for their livelihood. Farmers are willing to pay any royalty fixed by the Government for this purpose. There is an urgent need to simplify of procedure for getting permission keeping in view of problems being faced by farmers.

Sir, we all know that farmers are facing great difficulties. So, I request the hon. Finance Minister to waive off the interest on loans borrowed by the farmers.

Sir, regarding health care, I would like to state that in several hospitals, especially in Bellary, Karnataka, no medicines are available and number of doctors are very much shortage in Primary Health Centres. The large numbers of patients are facing hardships because of this non-availability of medicines and doctors. The amount, which the Union Government has allocated for health care facilities are not sufficient and there is an urgent need to increase the funds for this purpose.

Sir, there is one Ayurvedic hospital functioning in Bellary, Karnataka and this is the only hospital functioning in this area. This hospital is functioning in an old building, and it requires a new building. For this purpose, a sum of Rs. 5 crore is required. If this amount is released by the Central Government as grant, this hospital can develop its functioning, and it will be beneficial for patients also. Hence, I urge upon the Minister to release a sum of Rs. 5 crore towards grant for this hospital for the benefit of public at large.

The Government is manufacturing landline telephone instruments and the cell phone instruments are being manufactured by the private manufactures. The private manufacturers are charging heavy amount for these cell phone instruments, which causes great loss to the cell phone users. I urge upon the Union Government that the Government should also manufacture the cell phone instruments, and the instruments should be sold in normal prices. This would enable the people to purchase the cell phone instruments at cheaper rates.

*SARDAR RATAN SINGH AJNALA (TARAN TARAN): Sir, I have gone through the entire dget very minutely. The people of Punjab who live in border areas have been badly cheated in this Budget. The border districts of Gurdaspur, Amritsar and Ferozepur have been totally neglected and ignored in this Budget. Whenever there is war against Pakistan as in 1965 and 1971, the people of border areas act as second line of defence along with our soldiers. But when these people need help the Central Government conveniently ignores them. I am sad to note these developments. Mr Deputy Speaker Sir, earlier, when the NDA Government under the leadership of Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee was in power, the farmers whose land fell beyond the barbed wire fence were granted compensation at the rate of Rs 2500 per acre but this Government has stopped all compensation to such farmers. The present Central Government does not want to help the people of border areas. No package for any industry has been granted in these three border districts. In fact, there are no industries in these districts. In Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh the industries are not required to pay any taxes. So I would appeal to the Finance Minister that a special package for industries in the border areas should be granted so that these people should be bailed out. We, the people of the border areas, should be made to feel a part of India. We should be granted facilities as we are Indians. People of border areas are being ignored. It is the same story in the field of education. Schools are there in border areas. But no teachers are there in these schools. How can the poor children of these areas get education? The ten to fifteen kilometre border belt should be administered directly by Centre and special care should be taken regarding the needs of the people of border areas. For the last three years, about 750 acre land is in the possession of army. We have asked for compensation many times but no compensation has been 

* Translated of the speech originally delivered in Punjabi.

granted. The poor farmers have lost their land to the army. So I would appeal to the hon. Minister that compensation should be granted for this land under the possession of army. Deputy Speaker Sir, we, the border area residents do not have any phone facility. When we demand telephones, security concerns are cited. So some such provision should be made whereby they too can avail phone facility and feel a part of India. So my appeal to you is that the Government should look into this matter. Education facilities should be provided to them. Sir, the BSF people do not allow the farmers to go and tend their land that falls beyond the barbed wire fence, for more hours. The farmers are forced to work at BSF post without being paid. Only then are they allowed to go to their land. No irrigation facilities are there. No lighting facilities are there. People are very poor. So I appeal to hon. Finance Minister that some provisions should be made for people of border areas also, so that we too should feel part of this country and development of our area should also become a reality. THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, I am grateful to the hon. Members for this wide-ranging debate spread over nearly 15 or 16 hours. The debate was initiated by my hon. friend Prof. Vijay Kumar Malhotra from the Opposition Benches and my young friend Mr. Jyotiraditya Scindia from the Treasury Benches. 

Mr. Malhotra, I thought, was rather despondent, pessimistic and cynic. Jyotir on the other hand was confident, optimistic and proud to be able to support this Budget. I think it was a function only of their respective ages. But, I think, it is a function of where they sit and what they see. 

Last year, I did not have an opportunity nor did you have an opportunity to debate the Budget. We have made considerable progress this year, at least the Budget is being debated and discussed today. But, from what we all heard, there are no major issues. It was a muted debate. 

In fact, by and large, the only complaint I heard was pleased I think, that is a measure of success of the Budget rather than a measure of failure of the Budget. In fact, when I read the Budget Speech for 1 hour and 45 minutes until my friend Shri Harin Pathak rose as if a tsunami had hit him, everybody was quite happy to listen to the announcements made, to the vision that was being projected, to the allocations made and to the ideas that were being articulated. I think, the same sense prevailed over the last three days and I am truly grateful to all sections of the House for the broad support that they have extended to the Budget.

Sir, I do not intend to make a long speech. The Budget Speech is there. There is an Action Taken Report. I just want to draw your attention to the Action Taken Report. This is an innovation which the NDA Government started, and I compliment them for that, but it is a practice that we have continued. I think, if hon. Members will take a few minutes tonight or tomorrow morning to read this Report carefully, they will find that all but two or three announcements made in the last Budget have been implemented and even those one or two are under implementation. There are some administrative problems, but I am confident that even they will be implemented before 31st March, 2005. So, when I write a Budget Speech, when I read a Budget Speech, I have to be very conscious that next year I will have to come back and place before you another Report showing what we have done, how much we have accomplished, and therefore, there is no scope for making tall promises any more. 

In fact, I am happy that a certain realism has come to play a big part in making Budgets, in supporting Budgets and in criticising Budgets. We can no longer afford to make tall promises. This country has great capacity and potential, but this capacity and potential can be realised only if we subscribe to some fundamental principles of economics and economic growth. As I said in my Budget Speech, what permeate through this Budget are the principles of growth, stability and equity. Why do I put growth first? If this economy had not grown by 6.9 per cent or 7 per cent this year, there would simply be no money to provide for what we want to do next year. That I thought is so fundamental, but it bears repetition that without growth, there can be very little equity. It is, therefore, very important that all of us focus our attention on growth. 

If the economy grows by 7 per cent, you will have so much more money for whatever you want to do; if the economy grows by 8 per cent, you will have even more money for what you want to do; but if growth dips to 5 per cent or 5.5 per cent or growth is uneven like it was between 1999 and 2002, you will not have the funds, you will not have the money to do all that has to be done. Growth must be stable and sustainable. We cannot spend our way to growth. We cannot borrow our way to growth. Growth must be sustainable. It is, therefore, very important that we strike a right balance between taxes and borrowing, a right balance between taxes and savings, a right balance between lending rates and borrowing rates, a right balance between Plan expenditure and Non-Plan expenditure and a right balance between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.

If we emphasise on one and ignore the other, then you might have growth on the short run, but it will be an unstable and unsustainable growth. The primary emphasis in this Budget is on growth, but it must be a stable and sustainable growth. Believe me, if we can assure five years of stable and sustainable growth, then you will find that at the end of five years far more equity is achieved in this country than ever before, and so much more money will be available for all the projects that are so dear to our hearts. 

I believe, I have not strayed from the National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP). In fact, even those who feared that I might stray from the NCMP, now grudgingly concede that I have adhered pretty close to the NCMP. 

I have given these figures in the Budget speech. We have increased the allocation for the NCMP alone by Rs. 25,000 crore, that is, from Rs. 50,000 crore to Rs. 75,000 crore. This would not have been possible unless the UPA Government was firmly committed to the NCMP, and was willing to make any sacrifice in order to achieve the NCMP objectives. I assure you that if we have high growth this year, then again next year, that is, in 2006-2007, you will find that even more funds are allocated to the NCMP, so that we get nearer to our goals.

Sir, there was some criticism or some suggestion that investment is not taking place. Now, how do you make that statement? In fact, every commentator has noted that after an investment famine, perhaps famine is too strong a word, investment drought of about two years or two and a half years, it was in 2004-2005 that investment has sharply picked-up. 

We all get our numbers from the same sources. The NDA also got the numbers from the same source when it was in office. These are Reserve Bank figures, and figures of the Central Statistical Organisation (CSO). The best measure for investment is the non-food credit. Non-food credit in February 2004 was Rs. 7,75,697 crore. I have got figures for March, but I do not have comparable figures for March. Hence, I am reading February figures. In February 2005, this has increased to Rs. 10,07,801 crore, which means new investment of Rs. 2,32,104 crore has taken place in a period of 12 months.

Another measure is with regard to the bank credit. The bank credit during the same period has increased by Rs. 2,39,784 crore. I would urge the hon. Members to please visit the Parliament Library and read the RBI’s bulletin, which tells you where this money is going. This money is going into manufacturing; this money is going into infrastructure; this money is going into services; and this money is going into trade. For the first time, after many many months, we today have a sharp spurt in investment. I am not claiming the credit for it. All I am saying is that we have a good situation. We have a situation where the industry, trade, services are confident that they can invest, and earn a return on their investment. Let us not do anything, which will spoil this atmosphere. Let us encourage them to invest because it is investment alone, which will bring growth to this country, and growth alone will lead to greater equity. 

Sir, I have also other figures of investment. For example, these are think-tanks, which monitor investment sector-wise. For the first time you will find -- if you look at the figures from October to October -- that by October 2004, trends in total investment met by industry has risen over the year from October 2003 to October 2004 from Rs. 14,13,698 crore to Rs. 17,93,979 crore, which broadly supports the RBI figures.

Today, we are on the rising curve of investment. I believe, if we are able to manage the macro economic situation, well, without allowing for any hiccups or any disturbances, the year that will begin a few days from today, the 1st of April, 2005 (2005-2006) promises to be another good year. I am confident the UPA Government will be able to deliver another year of growth of more than seven per cent.

Sir, we are going to watch very carefully investment that takes place in agriculture, in irrigation and in water resources. We are going to monitor both public investment and private investment. We are carefully monitoring investment in manufacturing. There is a National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council; there is an Investment Commission; both of them will look closely at the investments in manufacturing, industry-wise and sector-wise. We will also look at investment in infrastructure. Here, of course, the leading role has to be played by the State. In power, in telecom, in roads, in airports, in seaports, the leading role will be played by the State sector; the supporting role will, indeed, be played by the private sector. But we are going to monitor very carefully the investment that takes place in infrastructure. Finally, we are going to monitor very carefully the investment that takes place in education and healthcare where the major role again will be by the State.

Sir, I do not intend to discuss the Finance Bill now; there will be another debate. I just want to make a statement on taxation. Taxes have two purposes. To levy, a tax or the rate of tax or the target of your tax must be so carefully designed that it raises revenues but it also promotes savings. If you tax too much, savings will be affected. If you tax too little, the State will have little revenue in order to spend for its proposals. My approach to taxation, the UPA’s approach to taxation, is – as NCMP says: "Tax rates will be moderate and stable." When we said that in May, it is because we believed that the tax rates in the earlier regime were not moderate. Otherwise, why should we use the word moderate? Rs. 75,000 crores have been allocated to the programmes of NCMP as against about Rs.50,000 crore in the current year. It is a sharp increase. But what is important is not outlays but outcomes. I think the most important passage in the Budget speech is paragraph 100. In the past, we have all been fascinated and carried away by outlays. Outlays are there but they must be translated to outcomes. So, what we have done is we are asking every Ministry to convert these outlays into outcomes. I am happy to report to you that the Prime Minister has written a letter to all Ministries and all Ministers requesting them that at the end of this month, we must convert outlays to outcomes and report to him. SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, we are all one in rejecting jobless growths. Jobless growth, I think, will do great harm to this country. We all agree on that. So, in the Budget speech I had identified the sectors that are likely to throw up the highest number of jobs. I think all of us can agree on those sectors also. What we intend to do in the course of the year, working with the Ministry concerned - the Ministry of Textiles, the Ministry of Biotechnology, the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers, the Ministry of Industry, the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, the Ministry of Mining, the Ministry of Tourism. What we intend to do during the course of the year is to closely monitor the investments that are taking place in that sector and the jobs that are being created in that sector.

Now that we have identified the sectors which have the highest job creating potential, you will find that through the year, Ministries and Departments are actively interacting with the stakeholders in that sector, investors in that sector to ensure that not only investments take place but investments translate to jobs.

There is a lot more to be done. On this I want to take about two or three minutes. There are at least half a dozen areas where Parliament as a body and Members of Parliament have to exercise great oversight. Otherwise, we fail. What are these? These are the Food for Work Programme, which during the course of this year, will become, when the Bill is passed, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme. Hon. Members said, we are confusing one for the other. We are not. At the moment, it is the Food for Work Programme. When the Bill is passed and becomes a low, it will become the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme. But this programme will succeed only if

design is correct and if the implementation is correct. Otherwise, it will be pouring money into a bottomless pit.

Similarly, the National Rural Health Mission will be launched on the 1st of April. The focus is on Government and community health system. An hon. Member asked: "Are you abdicating the responsibility?" Far from it. What we are doing is, while the State will bear the responsibility for the financial outlay, the community will have to own the system. The community will have to accept ownership of the system so that the system is accountable to the community. Today, the hospital and dispensary systems are accountable to no one. Some e Director, Medical Services is sitting at some State Capital. 

Now take the ICDS Programme. How will the ICDS succeed unless we can physically count by the end of the year 1,88,168 Anganwadis I know in some places, Anganwadis  are simply ghost centres. But we cannot delude ourselves by saying that we have provided the money and Anganwadi  is there. But there is neither an Anganwadi nor a mentor, nor children. We should be, physically at the end of the year, able to say that we have actually set up 1,88,168 Anganwadis. 

Now, I will come to Mid-day Meal Scheme. Hon. Member has said that ration is rather small. I will look into it. But over the years, in Tamil Nadu, the Mid-day Meal Scheme is a remarkable success. We have to make it a success. It is the largest feeding programme in the history of mankind. At no time in human history has 11 crore children been fed. We are making an attempt. There are shortfalls. There are deficiencies. I am not denying that. People have to set up kitchens; they will have to ensure the logistics; they will have to ensure supply of rice or wheat or oil or vegetables. It will take time. Kamraj took almost five to six years to build Mid-Day Meal Scheme. Therefore, States have a great responsibility. But when they succeed, believe me, this will be the largest feeding programme ever, 11 crore children will be given a meal.

Then, take the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. What is plaguing the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan? What is plaguing the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is absenteeism. There are reports which show that absenteeism of teachers in Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan  in the education system is as much as 20 to 25 per cent. Even when teachers attend schools, the teaching hours are no more than two to three hours. Then the backward regions need funds. We are putting aside Rs.5,000 crore every year and we will do so for five years in order to ensure that the backward regions of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, some parts of Andhra Pradesh and some other States which are listed – 170 districts have been identified by the Planning Commission – will get more funds. But all this will succeed only if the design of the programme is good, if the implementation is in good hands and we are able to measure outcomes at the end of the year. These are ambitious pogrammes. These are programmes of which we can be truly proud of, if at the end of the year, we can say that we have achieved substantially what we set out to achieve in the beginning of the year. 

There were some questions raised about Bharat Nirman. Bharat Nirman is not a pipe dream. Bharat Nirman is a business plan, and we are approaching it in a business like manner. I have listed what Bharat Nirman said. We have also set the goals, we have set for ourselves a four year business plan. I am confident that we will achieve, if I may paraphrase Jawaharlal Nehru’s words, if not fully, at least substantially, what we set out to achieve. The aim of the Bharat Nirman is to bring additional one crore hectare under assured irrigation. Irrigation is a subject which falls within the States’ jurisdiction, but we are providing money. States also provide money from their Budget. At the rate of about Rs. 75,000 per hectare for major and medium irrigation and Rs.50,000 per hectare for minor irrigation, we would require about Rs.67,500 crore. In 2003-04, State Governments with their own funds as well as funds provided by the Central Government have incurred a capital expenditure of about Rs.12,000 crore on irrigation. At this level of spending, it is safe to assume that Rs.50,000 crore is available. Now we will have to find another Rs.17,500 crore. It is not difficult, it is not impossible. We can find this money, and I am confident that over a period of four years, we will substantially achieve the target we have set for ourselves in irrigation. 

The next goal is to connect all villages with a population of 1,000 with a road.

Now, this programme requires an average of about Rs. 8,000 crore per year. There is a resource gap if you look at only the Central funds. But if we add the State funds, and the States are also spending on roads and bridges, my calculation shows that it is possible between the State funds and the Central funds to find this money of Rs. 8,000 crore per year in order to connect all villages with the population of 1,000.

The third goal is under Indira Awas Yojana – 60 lakh additional houses. This, in fact, is eminently achievable. We are in a position to build 15 lakh houses a year, and in four years, there is enough money to build 60 lakh houses, and, we will achieve this goal.

The fourth goal is to provide drinking water supply to the remaining 74,000 habitations. Now, the uncovered habitations require Rs. 15,300 crore. Then, there is a problem of water quality, which requires additional money in the eastern part of India. The programme requires an average of about Rs. 6,560 crore. If you take the Central Government’s allocations of about Rs. 4,050 crore and add to it what the States are spending -- going by last year’s figures -- there is enough money available to achieve this target also.

The fifth goal is telephone connectivity. This is eminently achievable. For, 66,822 villages, there is a universal service obligation. There is a very resurgent private sector. In fact, of all the six targets, the one that is most likely to be achieved ahead of the target is telephone connectivity. The one that is of problem is the rural electrification. There is a resource gap there, and I admit it. But that just does not mean we cannot set a target. We have set a target. There is a resource gap. We will be able to find the resources. I will make efforts to find the resources.

So, Bharat Nirman, if you approach, it is business plan. If States join with us and implement it as a business plan, I believe, Sir, that we can achieve substantially what we have set for ourselves in the four years, and, I am confident that the UPA Government’s report, at the end of five years, will show that Bharat Nirman has been substantially achieved.

Sir, let me just list new initiatives which were not mentioned in the debate. NHDP-I and NHDP-II were started by the NDA Government. But the NHAI goes back even before the NDA Government; I will come to that in a moment. But the NHDP-III is a new initiative of this Government. The Rs. 10,000 crore Special Purpose Vehicle for infrastructure is a very innovative idea of this Government. The National Urban Renewal Mission for the seven mega cities and all major towns is another major initiative, and my pet dream that we must have a world class university in India, and one of them, at least, must be by world class, is a new idea of this Government. I am confident that this year we will make a beginning, and we will show that we have made progress in these new initiatives.

Sir, I just want to say one or two words about some special points mentioned. But first, I want to deal with NHAI. There was some criticism that we have abandoned something about which Mr. Atal Bihari Vajpayee was very passionately committed to. Not at all. In fact, our commitment to roads goes even before the NDA came into office. The NHAI, I believe and if you recall, was set up by an Act of Parliament in 1988.

SHRI HARIN PATHAK : But nothing was done.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Just listen to me. It was set up in 1988. Now, during the period 12.12.2000 to 21.05.2004 -- I am sure, you remember the date, 21.05.2004, it is a very important date for all of you there -- you built four-laning 2,342 kilometres, and the average was 1.86 kilometres a day.

SHRI HARIN PATHAK : No, Sir. It was 11 kilometres per day… (Interruptions)

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Just listen to me.… (Interruptions)

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Please, listen to the hon. Minister.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Please listen to me. It was 2,342 kilometres under NHDP phase-I over a period of 1,257 days. If you divide 2,342 by 1,257 -- whether I divide it or you divide it -- the result is 1.86 kilometres per day.

As far as four-laning is concerned, under our Government, from 22.05.04 to 31.01.05, in a matter of 255 days, we have done 1,921 kms., an average of 7.53 kms. a day. Why do you say that we are not committed? … (Interruptions)

SHRI KHARABELA SWAIN : You are a very intelligent man! … (Interruptions)

SHRI HARIN PATHAK : You are manipulating with the figures. I will prove how we have done 11 kms. a day. … (Interruptions)

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Not to be recorded.

(Interruptions)* … 

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Please listen to me. … (Interruptions) All that you must know is this.

Sir, during 2003-04, the target fixed by the Government, according to the records given to me, was Rs.2,195 crore to be spent. They actually spent only Rs.1,340 crore. In 2004-05, we are going to spend Rs.2,155 crore. All that I am saying is that while you did start NHDP in the manner in which it is now being implemented, for which I compliment you, please acknowledge that this Government is continuing it with even much greater vigour than the previous Government. That is the point that I am trying to say.

There were some comments about how much did I recover in arrears of taxes. I do not want to take your time. I will deal with that when we deal with the Finance Bill. Just take it from me that the figures are there; we have recovered more as arrears of taxes in the current year than in any year before. I will give you the figures later.

* Not Recorded.

There were some questions about jute. I may not have mentioned jute, especially in my Budget speech, but I believe it is a part of the textile sector. We have before us, a very detailed proposal on jute. I want to assure the jute-growing States that these proposals are under our active consideration, and when we take decisions, I will report to Parliament. Jute is not far from our mind. In fact, it is very central to us, in terms of number of people employed, the number of secondary jobs created, the number of workers involved and the number of farmers involved there. I have a detailed note on jute. We are looking into the matter, and we will come back and tell you what we intend to do in jute.

On small-scale industries again, there is a popular misconception that the small-scale industries are dying. I concede that some SSI units may close down. But on the other hand, SSI units also have been opened. SSI units are also thriving. Let us look at the figures. These figures are complimentary both to you and me; there is no reason to apportion blame or share glory.

In 2000-01, there was a total of 101 lakh SSI units; in 2004-05, the number has increased to 118 lakh SSI units; the production has increased from Rs.2,61,289 crore to Rs.3,99,020 crore. The employment has increased from 239 lakhs to 282 lakhs. Exports have grown. I have only figures for three years, up to 2002-03. From Rs. 69,797 crore it has grown to Rs.86,013 crore.

I am not saying that SSIs do not face problems. I know that SSIs face problems. But SSI is a thriving sector. We have announced initiatives in the Budget. In the last Budget, I had announced initiatives. We have a Bill which will be coming on small and medium enterprises. Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill is coming in this Session. When that Bill is debated, the Minister would explain; if there is a chance, some of us will intervene and explain to you what we are doing in SSI. 

But let me once again tell all those who are engaged in SSI, those who are listening to the speech now – the entrepreneurs, promoters and workers – that this Government understands the key place of SSI units in India. We want them to become small and medium enterprises. There is a huge job creating potential in small and medium enterprises. The UPA Government will strain every nerve to make the small and medium enterprises sector a thriving sector.

*m76

All I would urge you is, go back and read Shri Yashwant Sinha''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''s speeches.

Sir, I want to conclude by appealing to all Members please pay attention to half a dozen areas where I want the States to act. The Government of India is largely a provider of funds, a provider of ideas. But implementation must be in the States. This Budget, as any other Budget, will succeed or fail only if the States cooperate, and I want, Sir, to appeal to the States, through you and through this House, first States must improve governance. Governance standards fall in the States, all the well-laid plans of men and mice will come to an end. Governance standards must improve in the States. When money is allocated to any particular programme, States must spend the money for that programme and not divert to any other programme. What we find is money is allocated to one programme, it is diverted to some other programme. We give it to Indira Aavas Yojana, it goes to something else. We give it for Pradhan Mantri Gram Sarak Yojana, it goes to something else. We give it for rural health care, it goes to something else. This 

happens in every State. I think States must spend the money for programmes for which they are allocated.

Thirdly, I appeal to all States, please honour the promise made by their Chief Ministers, honour the promise made by their Finance Ministers and implement VAT. It is good for India. Sir, 113 countries are implementing VAT. Implement VAT. It will make Indian taxation system at State level a modern and efficient taxation system.

Fourthly, amend your APMC Acts. APMC Acts are completely outdated Acts. We have today announced a programme, under the Ministry of Agriculture, Conditions upon that APMC Acts would be amended. Half a dozen States have amended the Acts. We are now living in the year 2005. The farmer today is not the farmer of 40 years ago. APMC Acts are outdated Acts. I would appeal to the States to amend their APMC Acts and take the benefit of the new schemes floated by the Ministry of Agriculture.

You work with the Government in implementing the Vaidyanathan Committee Report. The entire cooperative credit structure is in a shambles today. The Vaidyanathan Committee has recommended a huge amount of money to be outlayed and spent to revitalise cooperative institution. I am confident I can persuade the Prime Minister. I can persuade the Cabinet to give us the money and I can come back to you and ask you to vote for the money. Unless governance improves in the cooperative institutions, unless the legal structure is proper, unless the management structure is proper, unless there is no political interference in cooperative institutions, what is the point of spending Rs.15,000 crore? When we call a meeting of the State… (Interruptions)

SHRI HARIN PATHAK : RBI should do something.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: RBI is one which initiated this. When we call a meeting of the State Governments to implement the Vaidyanathan Committee Report, I would urge hon. Members to prevail upon their State Governments to work with us so that we can revive and save this cooperative institution which has done yeoman service in the past.

Finally, States must reduce the cost of lending by cooperative banks. Public sector banks are being urged to reduce their lending rates. It was 9 per cent during NDA Government; 8.5 per cent in the current year and I intend to take steps to see that those interest rates are brought down to the extent possible. For, on the one hand public sector banks are lending at 8.5 per cent, cooperative banks are lending at 12 per cent. There are good exceptions. There are half a dozen States where the State is bearing a part of the subsidy and lending it about six or six and a half per cent. But States must improve the management of cooperative banks, reduce the spread so that lending to farmers by cooperative institutions comes to an acceptable lending rates.

Finally, I would appeal to the States on this point. One of the most important initiatives, which irrespective of Government, has gathered pace and strength is a Self-Help Group. We have a major initiative for Self-Help Group for micro finance institutions. We will have a regulator for micro finance institutions. Self-Help Groups have taken wings now. In fact, women are doing a remarkable job. We have Women Self-Help Groups where the rate of recovery is 99 per cent which shows that when the women of India organise themselves and borrow money, place honour and pride not only in borrowing but in repaying the loan.

We are going to give a big boost to Self-Help Groups. We are going to give a big boost to micro finance institutions so that credit is available even for small and tiny enterprises. This will create jobs and income. So, I believe the philosophy of the Budget is based on the investment, growth, stability and equity. Having accepted that there is manpower shortage, the reply actually tells us nothing as to why the Government has been sitting on this matter. Shortage of manpower, specially sanctioned manpower, is an extremely serious matter. While on the one hand, the Navy is suffering on account of their projects being delayed, on the other hand, and more importantly, eligible youths are still amongst the unemployed. I would like to know from the Minister whether any efficient recruitment policy is being put in place so that these shortages do not occur in future.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, I have admitted that there is a shortage in the civilian personnel in Navy. Perhaps, the hon. Member is aware of a decision which was taken by the earlier Government in 2001. While presenting the Budget for that year, the then Finance Minister declared that a decision had been taken to reduce 10 per cent of civilian officials/employees in various Departments of the Government of India. A formula was also adopted as to how the vacancies would be determined, which is, one-third of the vacancies would be filled in and that one-third number of the vacancies should not exceed one per cent of the total sanctioned manpower.

There is one point which the hon. Member will agree, and I also agree with him, that due to this formula, Navy is suffering because unlike the Army and unlike the Air Force, a very big contingent of the Naval personnel belongs to civilian categories. Therefore, we have approached the Finance Ministry to relax this because if we apply this formula, the Army and the Air Force are not affected to that extent, but the Navy is affected where almost 50 per cent of the total contingent belongs to civilian category who help in repairing ships and other equipment on the docks.

Therefore, this issue has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance and I can assure the hon. Member, and through you the House, that this matter will be sorted out.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: At one point of time it was thought that those who are retiring from the Army could be inducted into the parallel Central Paramilitary Forces and like that because a lot of service is left. (Q. No. 382)

SHRI ARJUN SETHI : There is no denying of the fact that the energy security is of paramount importance and should be given priority to ensure energy supply for the country. In this context what are the new initiatives the Government have undertaken which are intended to ensure that the country will not be held to ransom on energy supply? 

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: While the question itself related to pricing of petroleum production, I am happy to answer, with your permission, the hon. Member's supplementary. Firstly, we are attempting to greatly increase production from existing producing wells through techniques which are called Improved Oil Recovery (IOR) and Enhanced Oil Recovery(EOL) techniques. 

Secondly, under the different rounds of the new Exploration Licensing Policy, we are attempting to attract a much larger amount of foreign investment and encourage partnership between Indian and foreign companies to increase the acreages that come under exploration and production. 

Thirdly, we are attempting to find equity oil or gas as well as producing as well as prospective properties outside the country. By combination of all these, we hope to substantially increase the availability and assuredness of hydro carbon supplies to meet our requirements. In this context, I believe, special mention must be made of the proposals to lay pipelines from Iran to Pakistan to India, from Turkmenistan to Afghanistan and Pakistan to India and from Myanmar through Bangladesh into India.

SHRI ARJUN SETHI : As the hon. Minister has referred, the question is related to oil pricing, I would like to ask the question on oil pricing. 

My question is very specific and definite. In view of the prevailing volatility of the situation in the oil sector, whether the Government intends to increase the price of petroleum products. If so, what is the quantum of it? What is the price of each barrel and whether the Government has taken any decision in this regard?

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: The short answer is ‘no’. The Government have not taken a decision in this regard, but the matter is under active consideration. I am afraid, I will not be able to vouchsafe the decision of the Government to the hon. Member until the Government takes a decision in this regard.

SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL : The question is about increasing the price of petroleum products. The basic thing is that the production of the petroleum products in the country itself is short. It is hardly 27 per cent to 28 per cent. We need about 72 per cent of the petroleum products to be imported, which is of worth more than Rs.1,10,000 crore. The basic thing that has to be tackled by the Government of India is the alternative source of energy like bio-diesel. I agree that the Government has taken an initiative in this regard. I would like to ask the hon. Minister whether the Government is going to take a decision to increase the use of ethanol in petrol from five per cent to ten per cent. Similarly, the production of the bio-diesel, in the world in more than 40 countries, is more and in our country also we have initiated eight to ten steps. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the Ministry would give surety for the people who are producing bio-diesel.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Mr. Speaker, Sir, addressing myself to the first part of the question which was relevant, I would like to inform the hon. Member that not only are we a major importer of crude oil and a very small importer of petroleum products but we have also become a very significant exporter of petroleum products. In the year 2004-05, it is estimated, subject to final confirmation, that there are exports, in the first eleven months of the year, amounted to Rs.25,699 crore. If we take the full year, it is likely to be somewhere in the region of Rs.28,000 crore. I think, the House needs to recognise the fact that the Ministry of Petroleum is increasingly becoming an export-oriented Ministry and does not remain merely an import-oriented Ministry.

As regards ethanol, we have had detailed discussions on this. I am sure, the hon. Member is aware of the discussion we have had with the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA). We have sent the ISMA, a draft MoU regarding short supply of ethanol at reasonable prices. Their response is still awaited.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, this is a suggestion on which I am not competent to give a full response. But what I can assure the hon. Member is that we have been very, very careful about the petroleum prices. I would like to just share with the House that during the period March, 1998 to January, 2004, when the international crude prices rose by about 17.78 dollars a barrel, and the period April, 2004 to April, 2005, when the international crude prices – I am talking of the Indian basket -- have also risen by approximately the same amount, 17.43 dollars, we have to note that whereas the price of petrol was raised by Rs. 10.87 per litre, we have raised it by only Rs. 4.28 per litre. They raised it by 48 per cent, and we raised it by 13 per cent. About diesel price, they raised it by Rs. 11.49, which is an increase of 112 per cent whereas in our case we have increased it by Rs. 6.48 per cent, which is an increase of only 13 per cent. About kerosene price, they increased it by Rs. 6.49, which is an increase of 258 per cent whereas our increase is exactly zero, it is zero per cent. We have not raised it. For domestic LPG, they raised it by Rs. 105.60, which is an increase of 78 per cent, whereas we have increased it by only Rs. 53.15, which is just an increase of a mere 22 per cent.

MR. SPEAKER: Please put questions in the background of the Government’s announcement that no decision has been taken.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : Sir, the hon. Minister today said that they have not decided anything about increase in the prices. That is the clear statement that he has made.

MR. SPEAKER: Up till now.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : Up till now – till today, and tomorrow, he can do it.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Till 1135 hours today, there is no increase.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : I understand the heart of the Minister he is playing his cards close to his chest. He has to be like that because he is a Minister. 

There was an article which appeared in the Press about the report of the Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas, wherein it was stated that the domestic price is linked to the international prices, and the domestic price is linked to the taxation of the Central Government. On that issue, I am seeking a clarification.

Is the Minister aware that the report has been submitted by the Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas wherein it was stated that already in the Budget, in different ways, taxation has been levied on petroleum products which will yield the Government, an additional Rs.3,000 crore and this taxation will come to surface in course of time. That is also a way to increase the prices. Is the hon. Minister aware that there is a report like this and is he aware that there is a contention in the Standing Committee that already tax has been increased, which is not disclosed, to the extent that it yields Rs.3,000 crore to the Government?

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Yes. The Government is aware of the report of the Standing Committee; the Government is aware of the figures given by the Standing Committee; and the Government is taking those figures extremely seriously. We will look into what the Standing Committee has said with utmost care before arriving at a decision. 

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : That is not the issue.

MR. SPEAKER: He has answered it. You have referred to the Standing Committee’s report. He has clearly said that the Government will give utmost consideration to that.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : May I know whether tax has been levied?

MR. SPEAKER: How can he say that? He is not the Finance Minister.

SHRI GURUDAS DASGUPTA : But the Ministry knows. He is avoiding a reply to the Parliament.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas is aware of the changes in the tax structure with respect to customs duty and excise duty that has been announced in the Finance Bill, 2005. The implications thereof have been examined by the Standing Committee and we are examining those implications. We have made some assumptions ourselves. We are in discussion with the Ministry of Finance. All these will be crucial components of the decision-making process.

We need to consult a number of Ministries. I want to do it as quickly as possible. I cannot, possibly, indicate a time frame. 

SHRIMATI MINATI SEN : Sir, under the Cinematography Act 1952, all music and video albums are to be certified by the Central Board of Film Certification to ensure transmission of video suitable for unrestricted public exhibition. An inter-Ministerial Committee under Section 20 of the Cable Television Network Regulation Act, 1995 had been formed to look into violations of programme code. 

Does the Government think that programmes being transmitted in several channels of cable television, such as Fashion TV, are in conformity with the programme code? 

If not, what action has so far been taken by the Government to stop projection of such videos which are against all norms of Indian culture?

SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, music albums are subject to the process of clearance of the Censor Board. Having said that, we have found that some TV channels were guilty of telecasting censored bits as well and we have also noticed that some TV channels did not conform to the programme code. Therefore, recently, we suspended the permission of one channel named Cine World for 30 days and we gave notices to as many as nine music channels as to why their permission cannot be withdrawn or suspended or revoked. We also gave notice to one TV channel for showing porn as part of news. While we are engaged in the process of enacting law, our Inter-Ministerial Group is active in taking action and we want to strengthen this process.

Title: Statement regarding rail accident of Train No.9168 Up Varanasi-Ahmedabad Sabarmati Express with Up Goods train at Samlaya Station on Godhara-Vadodara sector of Western Railways on 21.4.2005. 

12.05 hrs.

STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER*

MR. SPEAKER: I now request the hon. Minister to make a statement.

As a matter of fact, I had instructed the Government to make a statement on the unfortunate railway accident. Mr. Velu may please make the statement.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): Sir, it is with deep anguish that I apprise the House of an unfortunate rear end collision that occurred between 9168 Up Varanasi -- Ahmedabad Sabarmati Express and Up Goods train at Samlaya station on Godhra -- Vadodara section of Western Railway's Vadodara Division at 0310 hours on 21.04.2005.

In this accident, train engine and 8 coaches of 9168 Up Sabarmati Express derailed of which 7 coaches have capsized. 

The casualties reported so far, as a result of this unfortunate accident, is killed 12, and injured about 100. The injured have been admitted to Sayaji Rao Hospital, Vadodara and other nearby hospitals. Stranded passengers have been cleared from the site of accident by running a special train. 

Accident Relief Medical Vans from Vadodara, Ratlam and Ahmedabad along with teams of doctors have been rushed to the accident site for immediate medical relief of injured passengers. On receipt of information, Shri Lalu Prasad, Minister for Railways has rushed to the site accompanied by Shri Narainbhai J. Rathwa, Minister of State for Railways, Chairman and Member Mechanical, Railway Board. General Manager, Western Railway and other senior officers from Western Railway Headquarters office and Vadodara rushed to site immediately to supervise relief and rescue operation. Commissioner of Railway 

*Also placed in Library, See LT 1927/05

Safety, Western Circle has also reached the site of accident and will be inquiring into this accident. 

On behalf of the Railways and myself, I express our deep condolences to the bereaved families and also express sincere sympathies to the injured. I trust the House will join me in extending heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. All possible help including financial will be extended to the bereaved families and the injured. I assure the House that strict action will be taken against those found guilty.

Title: Speaker made observation regarding regulation of raising matters of urgent public importance after Question Hour (‘Zero Hour’). 

12.18 hrs.

OBSERVATION BY THE SPEAKER

MR. SPEAKER: Now, hon. Members, as you are aware, the matter relating to regulation of, what is called, ‘Zero Hour’ has been engaging our attention for quite some time. Yesterday, I had convened a meeting of the hon. Leaders of Parties in Lok Sabha to discuss this matter. After deliberations on the issue, it was agreed that the matters of only urgent national and international importance, to be decided by the Speaker, should be allowed to be raised. To enable raising of matters in an orderly manner, it was suggested that such Members who were to be permitted by the Chair will be duly informed before 12 Noon. To facilitate scrutiny of the matters, the notices should be received up to 0930 hours instead of 1000 hours.

It was further agreed that the number of matters to be raised under Rule 377 be increased from 15 to 20 per day to enable more Members to raise their issues.

In pursuance of this decision, it is proposed that with effect from 25 of April, 2005:

The notices for raising matters of urgent public importance after Question Hour will be given by 0930 hours on the day on which the matter is proposed to be raised instead of 1000 hours as at present;

Notices will be scrutinised with reference to the national and international importance of the matter and Members who are to be permitted to raise their issues will be duly intimated before the commencement of the so-called ‘Zero Hour’;

After the aforesaid names are exhausted, time permitting, other Members may be permitted to raise their issues in the order to be decided by the Speaker; and

The number of matters under Rule 377 be raised from 15 per day, as at present, to 20 per day.

Kind cooperation of the hon. Members is solicited.

Title: Regarding tabling of the Reports of the Justice Phukan Commisson and the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). 

SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL (CHANDIGARH): Mr. Speaker, Sir, I want to make a submission.

MR. SPEAKER: I will call you.

SHRI L.K. ADVANI (GANDHINAGAR): Mr. Speaker, Sir, yesterday you kindly permitted me to raise the question of the Pukhan Commission Report and the CVC Report. The House is grateful to you for having advised the Government to place the Pukhan Commission Report on the Table of the House. I do not know when it will be placed, but I hope that it would be placed before this Session ends.

MR. SPEAKER: That is the direction I have given already.

SHRI L.K. ADVANI : Yes.

On the second issue, namely the CVC Report, because that too relate to several defence procurement contracts, the hon. Leader of the House, who is also the Defence Minister, referred to the fact that when the PAC had sought the CVC Report the earlier Government had claimed privilege and had not given that report. This is true and it is the Government’s right. Even this Government can claim privilege in respect of any matter relating to security. But as one of my colleagues pointed out yesterday itself, in so far as the CVC Report relating to defence contracts is concerned, this Government has made that a part of the affidavit submitted to the Supreme Court. Having done that and allowed that CVC Report to go in the public domain, it cannot deny Parliament the CVC Report. So, there is a basic difference.

Therefore, I plead with you to see that the CVC Report is also placed on the Table of the House before the House takes up the discussion. It is a technical matter. It is in the public domain. So, we can already refer to it by seeing the affidavit. But for the Defence Minister to say yesterday that because the earlier Government had claimed privilege in that regard and had not given the CVC Report to the PAC, we also do not propose to lay it on the Table of the House is not a correct stand. This is my plea. … (Interruptions)

SHRI BASU DEB ACHARIA (BANKURA): Mr. Speaker, Sir, I want to say something on this issue. … (Interruptions)

MR. SPEAKER: No discussion on this now. If you want to do it, it is entirely for you.

THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): Mr. Speaker, Sir, I want to make a submission.

MR. SPEAKER: Yes.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: I have to correct two points.

First of all, I did not say that I would not lay it. That is factually not correct. What I said was that the hon. Leader of the Opposition should explain as to what prompted them to claim privilege when it was asked by the Public Accounts Committee.

Mr. Speaker, Sir, you will recollect that the functioning of the Public Accounts Committee is given so much importance that a former Prime Minister of the country was sent to jail by this House for breach of privilege and the breach of privilege was related to obstruction created by the Prime Minister’s Office in collecting materials in connection with the discharge of the functioning of the Public Accounts Committee. Therefore, my respectful submission to the hon. Leader of the Opposition was that it requires a clarification from the Opposition Benches who occupied this side of the House at that point of time.

The second point which I would like to correct is, whatever is available in the affidavit is in the public domain. The hon. Members can use it. There is no harm in it, but it has to be kept in mind that it was not offered suo motu by the Ministry of Defence. The highest court of the country asked as to what action you have taken in respect of the C&AG’s Report and in respect of the Vigilance Commission’s Report. In response to a Public Interest Litigation case when the Supreme Court gave this direction to the Ministry of Defence, we submitted the factual parts, the action taken parts on the CVC Report. Except that nothing has been given. It is in the affidavit itself and it is available to hon. Members. … (Interruptions)

PROF. VIJAY KUMAR MALHOTRA (SOUTH DELHI): Mr. Speaker, Sir, what was said yesterday was a total ...*…* 

MR. SPEAKER: No; do not use such expression.

… (Interruptions)

MR. SPEAKER: No; you cannot say that.

PROF. VIJAY KUMAR MALHOTRA : No, Sir, he referred to the CVC Report yesterday. … (Interruptions)

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYA RANJAN DASMUNSI): Mr. Speaker, Sir, on matters of procedure … (Interruptions) This pertains to a matter of procedure. … (Interruptions)

SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL : Mr. Speaker, Sir, it should not go on record.

Title: Regarding safety of passengers travelling in mails and express trains in the country. 

SHRIMATI MINATI SEN (JALPAIGURI): Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways through you to the quality of work done by unskilled workers in certain sections of Indian Railways.

There have been frequent accidents, including today’s accident, taking place in different parts of India. As you know, on April 10, 2005, there was an accident in which one passenger escaped narrowly. … (Interruptions)

MR. SPEAKER: Please do not give details now.

SHRIMATI MINATI SEN : On April 10, 2005, a passenger on Howrah-Kalka Mail narrowly escaped and it was found that in the running train iron sheet was not provided the vestibule between two compartments but it was merely covered with cloth. Similarly, this month, the New Jalpaiguri bound Darjeeling Express collided with a truck at Shaktigarh near Burdhwan and the driver and khalassi were killed on the spot. On April 18, 644 gelatine sticks were found in the Upper Kachar Express. This shows the extreme negligence of duties by the railway authorities concerned. I urge upon the Government through you to take stringent action for negligence of duties against the authorities concerned.

Title: Non-payment of wages and other statutory dues to workers in Hindustan Cables Limtied, Bharat Opthalmic Gas Limited and Burn Standards Wagon Limited. 

SHRI BIKASH CHOWDHURY (ASANSOL): Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a very important matter. About 3,000 workmen of Hindustan Cables Limited, Bharat Opthalmic Gas Limited and Burn Standards Wagon Limited have not received their salaries for the last seven months. Their families are in deplorable and terrible conditions. They are facing a lot of problems. 

So, I would request the concerned Minister to expedite the payment of their wages, etc. At the same time, the viability of the Hindustan Cables Limited should be expedited within two or three months so that the production of the Hindustan Cables Limited be started at the earliest.

Title: Celebration of "World Earth Day" on 22.4.2005. 

SHRI P. KARUNAKARAN : Sir, 22nd April is the World Earth day which has become a most important aspect in the human life. The World Earth Day is being celebrated for the last 35 years. The organised form of this movement came into existence in 1997 at Kyoto, an important city in Japan. Now, 141 countries have signed the Kyoto Protocol. Unfortunately, big countries like USA and Australia have not yet signed it because of their selfish motive. 

I would like to quote here :

"The Kyoto Protocol is a legally binding agreement under which industrialist countries will reduce their collective emissions of Greenhouse gases to 5.2 per cent compared to 1990."

The climatic history of the Earth has been a history of great contrasts. Due to the Carbon Dioxide and other five Greenhouse gases, the environment and atmosphere of the world changed to a great extent. Take for example, the case of India. In India itself, the precious and marvellous monument, the Taj Mahal itself is under threat. 

We have thousands of rivers with abundance of water. Very famous rivers like the Ganges, the Yamuna and the Cauvery are all polluted. We have a very vast area of forests and mountains. But you can see that these forests are now being encroached and destroyed. 

MR. SPEAKER : Please conclude.

SHRI P. KARUNAKARAN : Sir, I find that a meeting was held by our hon. Prime Minister to assess the number of tigers whose number is decreasing just because there is no forest at all. 

13.00 hrs.

So, in this context, on this day, I request the Government to have a comprehensive legislation to protect our environment and give strict instructions to the State Governments. The survival of forests, rivers and fresh air is really the prerequisite of human life today. Since we are not having a sitting tomorrow, I have raised this issue today to have a legislation on this matter. 

MR. SPEAKER: Shri Kishan Singh Sangwan. 

… (Interruptions)

MR. SPEAKER: ‘Sir-sir' business will not help you. Give up this habit also. 

… (Interruptions)

Title: Discussion on the Demands for Grants No. 1 to 3 under the control of Ministry of Agriculture. (Not concluded). 

13.02 hrs. 

GENERAL BUDGET-2005-06 - DEMANDS FOR GRANTS

Ministry of Agriculture

MR. SPEAKER: Hon. Members, yesterday we had decided in the Business Advisory Committee that today the discussion on Agriculture will start at 1 p.m. and there will be no lunch hour. 

The House will now take up discussion and voting on Demand Nos. 1 to 3 relating to the Ministry of Agriculture.

Hon. Members present in the House whose Cut Motions to the Demands for Grants have been circulated may, if they desire to move their Cut Motions, send slips to the Table within 15 minutes indicating the serial numbers of the Cut Motions they would like to move. Only those Cut Motions will be treated as moved. 

A list showing the serial numbers of Cut Motions treated as moved will be put up on the Notice Board shortly thereafter. In case any Member finds any discrepancy in the list, he may kindly bring it to the notice of the officer at the Table immediately.

Motion moved :

"That the respective sums not exceeding the amounts on Revenue Account and Capital Account shown in the third column of the order paper be granted to the President, out of the Consolidated Fund of India, to complete the sums necessary to defray the charges that will come in course of payment during the year ending the 31st day of March, 2006, in respect of the heads of demands entered in the first column thereof against Demand Nos. 1 to 3 relating to the Ministry of Agriculture."

Shri Kailash Joshi to initiate the debate.

MR. SPEAKER: This is very unfortunate, Maj. Gen. Khanduri.
